title: How to use this manual
lead:
Read this page once. It will save you hours, and it explains
  one thing about this course that nothing else will tell you.

blocks.label: Read this before anything else
blocks.html:
This paper is generated from the CCODEL course manual. The lecturer produces the questions by feeding that manual to a model, exactly as he did for the two objective tests you have already seen, which is why those tests quote it almost word for word.

So the manual is the syllabus. Graphs, trees, Boolean algebra, posets and lattices are not in it, and older papers that asked about them are no longer a guide to what you will be asked. Those sections have been taken out of the cram sheet and the two past-paper lessons have been taken out of the reading plan.

What remains is the twelve modules of the manual: logic, sets, functions, sequences, proof, induction, counting, probability and recurrence. Learn those and you have the paper.

blocks.text: The thing you need to know first

blocks.html:
This course has an official course text of 161 pages, and the text is the exam. The lecturer generates the questions by feeding it to a model, which is how the two objective tests you have already sat were written, and it is why they quote the text almost word for word.

That was not always true. Every older paper leaned heavily on graph theory, trees, the properties of relations, ordered sets and Boolean algebra, none of which the text covers, and this crash course was originally built to teach those from zero. They are no longer worth your time. What the text contains is what you will be asked, and nothing else is.

Meanwhile, on the 2025/2026 paper, roughly two marks in every five come from exactly that missing material. A student who revises only the course text walks into the hall having never seen two fifths of the paper.

So this manual teaches both: everything the course text covers, and everything the papers demand that it does not. Wherever a topic falls in the second group, it is flagged like this, once, at the top of the section:

Not in the course text
The official 161-page text does not cover this topic at all, and the exam tests it every year. Everything you need is taught here from zero. If you go back to the course text to revise this, you will not find it. That is the text's gap, not yours.

blocks.text: How every past question is presented

blocks.html: Past questions are the whole point of a manual like this, and they are easy to present dishonestly. If a book tidies a question into its own neat prose, it has done the hardest half of the work for you, namely working out what is being asked, and left you only the arithmetic. Worse, it hides the examiner's habits of phrasing, which are exactly what you are training to recognise, and it quietly repairs the paper's own mistakes, so you never learn that papers contain mistakes.
This manual therefore never restates a past question. Every one arrives in three parts, in this order.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(2 marks)The examiner's exact words
      appear in a box like this one, carrying the paper's own numbering,
      spelling, symbols and mark text, down to the last comma.

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
If a question contains a typo, a contradiction or an ambiguity, it stays in the quote and is flagged here, underneath. It is never silently corrected, because when you meet it in the hall it will not have been corrected for you either. Handling a broken question is part of the skill.

Break it down
Given
what the question hands you, listed plainly.
Asked
what it actually wants. The instruction verb decides this, and it is where marks are most often thrown away: "state" is not "prove", "differentiate" is not "define", and "determine which is true" is not "convert".
Marks say
what the mark count tells you about the depth expected, and roughly how long to spend.
Teaches
the section of this manual that covers it.
Trap
the specific way people lose marks on this one.
Only then comes the worked answer. Questions this manual wrote itself, for practice, are labelled as practice and never wear an "As printed" bar, because they were never printed by anybody.

blocks.text: The boxes, and what each one is for

blocks.html: Navigate by shape and colour. Each box does exactly one job.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html: One idea, in plain language, built from what you already know. Never two ideas in one box.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Crimson appears nowhere else in this book. When you see it, the content is going into your memory, not just past your eyes. Each one carries a hook to make that easier.

Memory hook: crimson means learn this by heart.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working: A full solution with the reasoning shown on every line. The chip on the right names where the question came from, so you always know whether you are looking at a real exam question and which paper it is from. Numeric ones open by listing what you were given and what you must find, before any formula appears.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: The mistake made every year. Read these twice.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question: A question with its answer hidden below a dashed rule. Cover the answer, say yours out loud, then look. Reading the answer without trying first teaches you almost nothing, however productive it feels.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html: Cloze practice. Write the missing words on paper, not in your head.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.html: A program, with its real output, given in Python and C++. Every listing in this manual was run, and the output shown is what the machine actually printed, not what it ought to have printed.

Work with a pen and blank paper. When a worked example ends, cover it and redo it from the question. When you reach a past paper, sit it under exam conditions before you read a single answer: three hours, four questions, no notes. A paper you have read the answers to teaches you far less than one you have struggled through and then marked.

The parts are ordered so that nothing is used before it is taught. If you meet a symbol you do not recognise, it was introduced earlier, and the Formula and Notation Reference at the back lists every one.
The format changed part way through the papers we hold, so be careful with the older ones.

SessionCode printedInstructionTimeUnitsMarks per question
2020/2021CSC311Attempt any THREE2 hours223.5
2021/2022CSC416Attempt any THREE2 hours223.5
2023/2024CSC 242not on our copynot statednot stated23.5
2024/2025CSC416Attempt any FOUR3 hours317.5
2025/2026CSC 242Answer any Four (4)3 hours317.5

It is one course that has been renamed twice, so all five papers are valid practice. The current shape is the last row: six questions, answer any four, 17.5 marks each, 70 marks in three hours. That is about 44 minutes a question. This manual solves all five papers in full, then gives you three more in the current shape to sit.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
You choose four questions out of six, so it is tempting to plan on dodging a topic. Look at what that costs on the 2025/2026 paper: graphs appear in Q1, Q4, Q5 and Q6, and counting appears in Q3, Q4 and Q6. There is no set of four questions you can answer while avoiding graph theory, and no honest way to avoid counting either.

The choice protects you against a bad day on one topic. It does not let you leave one out.

title: What To Write, Step By Step, Whatever They Ask
lead: Nine recipes covering every kind of question the manual can generate. Name the question, find the recipe, follow it line by line.
blurb: A procedure for each question type on this paper, written as instructions you can execute cold.

blocks.label: How to use this page
blocks.html:
This paper is generated from the manual, so every question is one of nine kinds. Read it, decide which, follow that recipe.

If the question says...Use recipe
"Define", "What is", "Explain the term"1. Define
"Construct a truth table", "Is it a tautology"2. Truth table
"Show that P is equivalent to Q", "Simplify"3. Equivalence
"Write in symbols", "Negate the statement"4. Quantifiers
"Find A union B", "List the power set"5. Set operations
"Is f one-one / onto", "Find f of g"6. Functions
"Find the nth term", "How many terms"7. Sequences
"Prove by induction"8. Induction
"How many ways", "In how many arrangements"9. Counting
Three rules for every answer

1. Start a definition with the term and the word is.
2. Show the substitution before the arithmetic. The working carries marks even when the number is wrong.
3. State the formula you are using by name before you use it.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page, read, answer, slide down one line to check.

frames.teach: The first move is always to NAME the kind of question, not to start solving it.
frames.ask: A question says "In how many ways can 5 people be seated in a row?". Which recipe?

frames.check: Recipe 9, counting.
frames.teach: Anything asking HOW MANY WAYS is counting: product rule, permutation or combination.
frames.ask: "Show that not(P and Q) is equivalent to notP or notQ." Which recipe?

frames.check: Recipe 3, equivalence.
frames.teach: You may do it by truth table or by naming the law. Naming the law is faster and scores the same.
frames.ask: And what is the name of that particular law?

frames.check: De Morgan's law.
frames.teach: A question that gives you a formula and says "prove for all n" is always induction, and always earns marks for the base case alone.

blocks.label: Recipe 1. Define a term
blocks.html:
Step 1. Term, then is, then the category and what makes it different.

A tautology IS a compound proposition that is true for
every possible assignment of truth values to its variables.

Step 2. Add the contrast: a contradiction is false in every row, a contingency is neither.

Step 3. Give one tiny example. p or not p is a tautology.

Never leave a definition blank. Naming the category alone earns something.

blocks.label: Recipe 2. Construct a truth table
blocks.tag: "Construct a truth table", "Is it a tautology"
blocks.html:
Step 1. Count the variables. n variables means 2 to the power n rows. Two variables, four rows. Three variables, eight.

Step 2. Fill the variable columns mechanically, never by thinking:

p:  T T F F          p:  T T T T F F F F
q:  T F T F          q:  T T F F T T F F
                     r:  T F T F T F T F

Step 3. Add one column per connective, working from the innermost bracket outwards. Do NOT jump to the final column.

Step 4. Read the last column:

all T          -> TAUTOLOGY
all F          -> CONTRADICTION
mixed          -> CONTINGENCY
same as another column -> the two are EQUIVALENT
The four connective rules, in one place

AND is true only when both are true.
OR is false only when both are false.
IMPLIES is false only when true implies false.
IF AND ONLY IF is true when both sides agree.

blocks.label: Recipe 3. Show two statements are equivalent
blocks.html:
Two routes. Either is acceptable; the second is faster.

Route A, truth table. Build a column for each side and show the two columns are identical. Then write: the two columns agree in every row, therefore the statements are logically equivalent.

Route B, name the laws. Transform one side into the other, writing the law used beside each line:

not(p and q)
= not p or not q          De Morgan

The laws worth knowing by name:

LawWhat it says
De Morgannot(p and q) = not p or not q, and not(p or q) = not p and not q
Distributivep and (q or r) = (p and q) or (p and r)
Implicationp implies q = not p or q
Contrapositivep implies q = not q implies not p
Double negationnot(not p) = p
Identity, dominationp and T = p, p or T = T

If you cannot see which law applies, fall back to Route A. A correct truth table always scores.

blocks.label: Recipe 4. Quantifiers and negation
blocks.html:
Step 1. Identify the domain and the predicate. "All students passed" gives domain = students, P(x) = x passed.

Step 2. Choose the quantifier. All, every, each means the universal one. Some, there exists, at least one means the existential one.

Step 3. To NEGATE, apply the one rule that does all of it:

Swap the quantifier, and negate the inside.

not ( for all x, P(x) )    =    there exists x, not P(x)
not ( exists x, P(x) )     =    for all x, not P(x)

In words: the opposite of "everyone passed" is not "everyone failed", it is "someone did not pass". That is the marked point.

Step 4. If asked whether it is true, remember: a universal statement dies to ONE counterexample; an existential statement lives on ONE example.

blocks.label: Recipe 5. Set operations and power sets
blocks.tag: "Find A union B", "List the power set"
blocks.html:
Union: everything in either, listed once. Intersection: only what is in both. Difference A minus B: start with A, remove anything also in B. Complement: everything in the universal set not in A.

Power set, step by step. For a set with n elements there are 2 to the power n subsets, and listing them has an order that stops you missing any:

A = {a, b, c}          23 = 8 subsets

size 0:  { }
size 1:  {a}  {b}  {c}
size 2:  {a,b}  {a,c}  {b,c}
size 3:  {a,b,c}

Count them: 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8. Correct.

Always check your count against 2 to the n before moving on. That single check catches almost every mistake in this question type.

Cardinality of a union, when asked: |A union B| = |A| + |B| minus |A intersect B|. For three sets, add the singles, subtract the pairs, add the triple back.

blocks.label: Recipe 6. Functions
blocks.html:
Domain in, codomain allowed out, range actually out. Say that sentence before answering anything about functions.

Is it one-one (injective)? Ask: can two different inputs give the same output? If yes, it is NOT one-one, and you must give the pair as evidence. For x squared, 2 and minus 2 both give 4.

Is it onto (surjective)? Ask: is every element of the codomain hit? Equivalently, does range equal codomain?

Is it bijective? Both. And only then does an inverse exist.

Composition. g of f means apply f first. Substitute the whole of f into g:

f(x) = x + 1,  g(x) = 2x

g(f(x)) = 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2
f(g(x)) = 2x + 1          different, so order matters

How many functions from a set of m to a set of n? n to the power m. Test it on tiny numbers: 2 inputs into 3 outputs gives 3 squared = 9.

blocks.label: Recipe 7. Sequences and progressions
blocks.html:
Step 1. Name the sequence. Subtract consecutive terms; if constant, it is ARITHMETIC and that constant is d. Divide consecutive terms; if constant, it is GEOMETRIC and that constant is r.

Step 2. Write the formula by name before substituting.

Arithmetic   nth term:  a + (n - 1)d
             sum:       n/2 [ 2a + (n - 1)d ]

Geometric    nth term:  a rn-1
             sum:       a(rn - 1) / (r - 1)

Step 3. Write down a, d or r, and n explicitly before you substitute. Most lost marks here are from putting the wrong number in the wrong slot, not from the algebra.

Fibonacci is neither: each term is the sum of the two before it, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. If a question gives that pattern, say so and continue the sequence rather than hunting for d or r.

blocks.label: Recipe 8. Prove by induction
blocks.html:
Write these four headings on your script before you think. Each earns marks on its own.

BASE CASE
   Show it holds for n = 1. Substitute and check both
   sides give the same number. Say "true for n = 1".

INDUCTIVE HYPOTHESIS
   "Assume the statement is true for n = k", and write
   the statement out with k in place of n.

INDUCTIVE STEP
   Show it holds for n = k + 1. Write the k + 1 statement,
   then SUBSTITUTE the hypothesis into it.

CONCLUSION
   "By the principle of mathematical induction, the
   statement holds for all natural numbers n."
The move that makes the step work

In the step, you always take the sum to k + 1, split off the last term, and replace the sum to k with what the hypothesis says it equals. That substitution IS the proof; everything after it is algebra.

Never skip the base case even when it is obviously true. It is a separate mark.

blocks.label: Recipe 9. Counting
blocks.html:
Step 1. Does order matter? That one question chooses your formula.

SituationUse
Order matters, arrangingPermutation: nPr = n! / (n - r)!
Order does not matter, choosingCombination: nCr = n! / [ r!(n - r)! ]
Several stages, each with choicesProduct rule: multiply them
Either this OR that, no overlapSum rule: add them
All n arranged in a rown!

A committee is a combination, because swapping two members changes nothing. A password or a seating order is a permutation, because swapping changes it.

Step 2. Write the formula, then the substitution, then the number.

Choose 3 from 8, order irrelevant:

8C3 = 8! / (3! x 5!)
    = (8 x 7 x 6) / (3 x 2 x 1)
    = 336 / 6
    = 56

Binomial theorem, if asked to expand: the coefficients of (a + b) to the n are nC0, nC1, ... nCn, the powers of a fall from n to 0 and the powers of b rise from 0 to n, and there are n + 1 terms.

blocks.big: "Name the question, find the recipe, follow the steps, and show the substitution."
blocks.sub: Truth tables: 2 to the n rows, filled mechanically. Negation: swap the quantifier and negate inside. Power set: list by size and check against 2 to the n. Induction: base, hypothesis, step, conclusion, four headings. Counting: does order matter.

title: Numbers, Symbols and Notation
lead:
Discrete mathematics has a small vocabulary. Learn it once here
  and nothing later in this book will look like a foreign language.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will know what "discrete" means, be able to name and write the standard number sets, read and write the membership and subset symbols out loud, and use factorial and summation notation without hesitating.

blocks.text: What "discrete" means, and why the course exists

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: The one word in the title
blocks.html:
Discrete means separated, made of individual pieces you can count, with nothing in between. Its opposite is continuous, which flows without gaps.

The whole numbers 1, 2, 3 are discrete: between 2 and 3 there is no other whole number. Temperature is continuous: between 20 degrees and 21 there are infinitely many values, and you can always find another.

A computer is a discrete machine. It stores whole bits, executes whole instructions, and holds finitely many values. That is the whole reason this course exists: the mathematics of computing is the mathematics of things you can count and separate, not the mathematics of smooth curves.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Where each part goes in computing
blocks.html:
Keep this map in your head. It also answers a question the examiner likes to ask directly (2025/2026 Q2a asks for five justifications for including discrete structures in a computer science curriculum).

TopicWhat it is for in computing
LogicCircuit design, conditions in programs, database queries, proving a program correct, artificial intelligence
SetsData types, database tables, collections, search spaces
FunctionsEvery subprogram, hashing, encryption, compression
CountingAlgorithm complexity, password strength, probability of collisions
Proof and inductionShowing an algorithm always works, not just on the cases you tried
RecurrenceThe running time of a recursive algorithm

Graphs, trees and relations are deliberately absent from this map. They appear in older papers, but the CCODEL manual has twelve modules and none of them is graphs, trees, relations, posets or Boolean algebra, and the manual is what generates this paper.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(a) Provide five Justification the inclusion of Discrete structure to Computer Science
      students curriculum. (5 marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
A word is missing and one is capitalised mid-sentence. The sentence should read "Provide five justifications for the inclusion of discrete structures in the computer science students' curriculum". The meaning is not in doubt: give five reasons the subject belongs on the degree. Answer it as the five-reason question it is.

Break it down
Given
Nothing. This is an opinion question with a right answer.
Asked
Provide five justifications. The number is explicit, so give exactly five, numbered. Four costs a mark; six wastes time.
Marks say
5 marks, one per justification. Each wants a claim and a concrete example of where it bites. A bare list of topic names is not a justification.
Teaches
This section, F.1, using the table above.
Trap
Listing five topics ("logic, sets, graphs, trees, counting") instead of five reasons. The question asks why the subject is included, not what is in it.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Five justifications, each a claim with a concrete example attached.
blocks.working:
1. Computers are discrete machines, so discrete mathematics is their native mathematics. A machine stores whole bits and executes whole instructions; it has no smooth quantities. Continuous mathematics describes a falling stone, but nothing inside a processor. Example: an integer overflow is a fact about a finite set of representable values, and only discrete reasoning predicts it.
  2. It supplies the language in which algorithms are specified and their cost measured. Counting techniques give the running time of a procedure before it is ever run. Example: knowing that comparing every pair of n records takes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons tells you the method will not scale, without writing a line of code.
  3. It is the basis of correctness, not merely of testing. Logic and proof by induction establish that a program works for every input, where testing only covers the cases you thought of. Example: proving a loop invariant holds shows a sorting routine is right for all inputs, including the ones nobody tried.
  4. Its structures are the data structures of the subject. Sets, relations, functions, graphs and trees are not analogies for computing objects; they are those objects. Example: a relational database is built directly on relations, and a file system is a tree.
  5. It underpins the applied areas the degree leads to. Networking, cryptography, compilers and artificial intelligence all rest on it. Example: routing traffic is a shortest-path problem on a graph, and public-key cryptography rests on number theory over the integers.

How to write it under time pressure: number them 1 to 5, give each a bold opening claim and one sentence of example. Five short numbered paragraphs read as five justifications; one long paragraph reads as one.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
A set is any collection of distinct objects, gathered together and treated as one thing. Part Two studies sets properly; for now you only need the five standard ones, because every question in this course lives in one of them.

They are written with a special doubled letter so nobody confuses the set of all integers with a variable called Z.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
SymbolNameWhat is in it
ℕthe natural numbers0, 1, 2, 3, ... the counting numbers
ℤthe integers... −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ... whole numbers, positive and negative
ℚthe rational numbersanything writable as a fraction of two integers, such as 3/4 or −7
ℝthe real numbersevery point on the number line, including π and the square root of 2
ℂthe complex numbersreals extended with the square root of −1 (not examined here)

Memory hook: Natural, Zahlen (German for numbers, which is where ℤ comes from), Quotient, Real, Complex. Each doubled stroke says "this is a whole universe of numbers, not a variable".

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
Textbooks disagree. Some start the natural numbers at 0, some at 1. In computing, 0 is almost always included, and this manual includes it.

What matters in an exam: say which convention you are using. One short sentence ("taking ℕ to include 0") protects you completely, and a marker cannot penalise a stated convention. What loses marks is leaving it ambiguous and then relying on it.

blocks.text: Membership: the two symbols you will use most

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
To say that an object is in a set we write ∈. The statement 3 ∈ ℤ is read "3 is an element of the integers", or more casually "3 is in Z". The symbol is a stylised Greek epsilon, for the Greek word meaning "is".

To say an object is not in a set, strike it through: ∉. So ½ ∉ ℤ reads "one half is not an element of the integers", which is true, because one half is not a whole number.

The left side is always an object and the right side is always a set. That direction never changes, and it is the single most common slip in first attempts.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
WrittenSaidTrue?
5 ∈ ℕ5 is an element of the natural numbersyes
−5 ∈ ℕminus 5 is an element of the natural numbersno, ℕ has no negatives
−5 ∈ ℤminus 5 is an element of the integersyes
π ∉ ℚpi is not an element of the rationalsyes, pi is not a fraction
π ∈ ℝpi is an element of the realsyes

Memory hook: ∈ opens towards the set, like a mouth swallowing the element.

blocks.text: Two ways to describe a set

blocks.html: The 2025/2026 paper asks for exactly this, in two marks, so learn both names.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
1. The roster method, also called listing or the tabular method. Write the members out between braces, separated by commas.

A = {2, 4, 6, 8}

2. Set-builder notation, also called the rule method. State the property that decides membership.

A = {x | x is an even number and 0 < x < 10}

The vertical bar is read "such that". Some books use a colon instead, which means the same thing. The whole line is read: "A is the set of all x such that x is even and x is between 0 and 10".

Memory hook: the roster method names the members, the way a class register does. Set-builder gives the entry rule, the way a door policy does.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Write each set both ways.
blocks.working:
(a) The odd numbers under 10.
Roster: {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}.
Set-builder: {x | x ∈ ℕ, x is odd, x < 10}.

(b) The days of the week starting with T.
Roster: {Tuesday, Thursday}.
Set-builder: {d | d is a day of the week and d begins with T}.

(c) The integers whose square is 4.
Set-builder: {x | x ∈ ℤ and x² = 4}.
Roster: {−2, 2}. Notice the roster form does the work of solving the equation for you, which is exactly why an examiner asks for it.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: write "the prime numbers below 12" both ways, then check: {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.tag: Sets do not repeat and do not care about order
blocks.html:
{1, 2, 2, 3} is the same set as {1, 2, 3}. Writing an element twice adds nothing, because a set records only whether a thing is in.

{3, 1, 2} is also the same set as {1, 2, 3}. Order carries no information either.

This matters later. When order does matter you are no longer dealing with a set but with an ordered pair or a sequence, and the brackets change from braces to parentheses: (1, 2) is not (2, 1). Part Three is built entirely on that distinction.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
For a whole number n, n! (said "n factorial") means multiply every whole number from n down to 1.

n! = n × (n − 1) × (n − 2) × ... × 2 × 1

n a whole number, 0 or more. n! the product of every whole number from n down to 1. By definition 0! = 1.

The first few, which you should know on sight:

n01234567
n!1126241207205040

Memory hook: 0! = 1 looks wrong but is forced: there is exactly one way to arrange nothing, namely do nothing. Every counting formula in Part Five breaks if you set it to 0.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
10! is already 3 628 800, and 20! is bigger than a billion billion. This is not a curiosity: it is the reason some problems are hopeless to solve by trying every possibility. The travelling-salesman question in Part Six turns on exactly this.

Useful cancelling trick, used constantly in Part Five:

10! / 8! = (10 × 9 × 8!) / 8! = 10 × 9 = 90

Never expand both factorials and divide. Cancel first. It turns an impossible arithmetic problem into a two-second one.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
The Greek capital sigma, ∑, is shorthand for "add up". It is read "the sum of".

∑i=1n ai = a1 + a2 + ... + an

i the index, a counter. i=1 below the sigma, where the counter starts. n above the sigma, where it stops. ai the thing being added, written in terms of i.

So ∑i=14 i² means 1² + 2² + 3² + 4² = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30.

Memory hook: sigma is the Greek S, for Sum. Read it left to right as a sentence: "sum, from i equals 1, up to n, of a-sub-i".

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. Say out loud what 7 ∉ ℚ would mean, and say whether it is true.

2. What is 6! / 4!?

3. Write {x | x ∈ ℤ and −2 ≤ x ≤ 2} by the roster method.

4. Evaluate ∑i=13 (2i + 1).

Answers

1. "7 is not an element of the rationals". It is false: 7 = 7/1, so 7 is rational.
2. 6!/4! = 6 × 5 = 30. Cancel, do not expand.
3. {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2}.
4. (2+1) + (4+1) + (6+1) = 3 + 5 + 7 = 15.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. The symbol ∈ is read .
  2. ℤ is the set of .
  3. The two mathematical ways to describe a set are the method and notation.
  4. 0! equals .
  5. In set-builder notation the vertical bar is read .
Answers

1. is an element of. 2. the integers. 3. roster (listing), set-builder (rule). 4. 1. 5. such that.

title: Reading and Writing Mathematics
lead:
Mathematical English is a dialect. A handful of phrases mean
  something narrower than they do in ordinary speech, and marks are lost every
  year by reading them casually.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will know exactly what "if", "only if", "if and only if", "necessary" and "sufficient" translate to in symbols, what the instruction verbs on an exam paper demand, and how to lay out an answer so a marker can give you every mark you earned.

blocks.text: The five phrases that carry the marks

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Two arrows, before we use them
blocks.html:
Two symbols appear all through this section, so they are introduced here and studied properly in Part One.

→ is the implication, also called the conditional. p → q is read "if p then q", and it is a single statement claiming that whenever p holds, q holds too.

↔ is the biconditional. p ↔ q is read "p if and only if q", and it claims the two always hold together: each one implies the other. It points both ways because it works both ways.

Here p and q stand for whole statements. Section 1.1 gives them their exact truth tables; for now these readings are enough.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Take a statement of the form "if p then q", written p → q. English dresses it up in several ways, and they are not interchangeable.

p is sufficient for q. Having p is enough to guarantee q. Being a dog is sufficient for being an animal.

q is necessary for p. Without q you cannot have p. Being an animal is necessary for being a dog.

So one implication, p → q, says two things at once: p is enough, and q is required. Which side is which is the whole question, and it is the thing the examiner tests.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
EnglishSymbols
if p, then qp → q
p implies qp → q
q if pp → q
p only if qp → q
p is sufficient for qp → q
q is necessary for pp → q
q whenever pp → q
q unless not pp → q
p if and only if qp ↔ q
p is necessary and sufficient for qp ↔ q

Memory hook: the two dangerous ones are "p if q", which is q → p, and "p only if q", which is p → q. "If" alone introduces the hypothesis; "only if" introduces the conclusion. They point opposite ways.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.tag: "Whenever" and "only if" reverse people every year
blocks.html:
The 2024/2025 paper uses both, deliberately.

"I go to the beach whenever it is a sunny summer day." The "whenever" clause is the hypothesis. Let p be "it is a sunny summer day" and q "I go to the beach". This is p → q, not q → p. The sunny day triggers the beach trip, not the other way round.

"When I stay up late, it is necessary that I sleep until noon." Here "necessary" marks the conclusion. Let p be "I stay up late" and q "I sleep until noon". This is p → q.

Method that never fails: rewrite the sentence as a plain "if ... then ..." before you touch symbols. Do that in the margin, then translate. Two extra seconds, and the whole question stops being about English.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Translate each into symbols, with p = "it is raining", q = "the match is cancelled".
blocks.working:
(a) "The match is cancelled if it is raining."
Rewrite: if it is raining, then the match is cancelled. So p → q.

(b) "The match is cancelled only if it is raining."
"Only if" marks the conclusion, so rain is required for cancellation. Rewrite: if the match is cancelled, then it is raining. So q → p. Note that this is the reverse of (a), from a sentence that differs by one word.

(c) "Rain is necessary and sufficient for cancellation."
Both directions at once: p ↔ q.

(d) "The match is cancelled whenever it rains."
"Whenever" marks the hypothesis: p → q, the same as (a).
blocks.redo: Now redo it: translate "passing the exam is necessary for graduating". Answer below the fold of your hand: let g be graduating and e be passing, then g → e.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Read the verb before you start writing
blocks.html:
Marks are allocated to the verb, not to the topic. A perfect definition earns nothing when the question said "prove". This table is drawn from the verbs the five papers actually use.

VerbWhat earns the marks
DefineOne precise sentence. No example needed unless asked.
StateThe claim itself, in full, with its conditions. Not a worked instance of it.
ExplainThe idea in your own words, plus why it is so. Usually an example is expected.
Differentiate betweenA stated point of contrast, both sides, on the same axis. A list of two definitions side by side does not differentiate.
Show that / ProveAn argument that settles every case, not a check of one or two.
Determine whetherA verdict plus the reason. A bare yes or no scores almost nothing.
Construct / DrawThe object itself, labelled.
Compute / Calculate / FindThe number, with the working that produced it.
With the aid of examplesThe example is compulsory and carries marks of its own.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
The 2025/2026 paper opens with ten marks of "differentiate between the following", five pairs at two marks each. The commonest way to lose half of those ten marks is to write two definitions and stop.

A contrast needs a shared axis. Compare this pair of answers on the two ways of describing a set, from F.1:

Scores poorly: "The roster method lists the elements. Set-builder notation uses a rule."

Scores fully: "Both name exactly the same collection, and either can describe any set that the other can. They differ in what they make easy. The roster method writes the members out, so it is direct but only practical for a small finite set: {2, 4, 6, 8}. Set-builder states the property that decides membership, so it handles infinite sets and sets defined by a condition: {x | x is even and 0 < x < 10}. The roster shows you what is in; set-builder shows you why."

Same facts. The second one answers the verb, because every sentence contrasts the two on a stated axis: what they name, what they make easy, what they show.

blocks.text: How to lay out an answer

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
For anything with a number in it, write these four things, in this order, every time.

1. Given. The values the question handed you, listed.
2. Find. What is being asked, in your own words.
3. Formula or rule. Stated before it is used, with what each letter means.
4. Substitute, work, and answer. With units or a unit of counting.

This is worth real marks even when your arithmetic goes wrong, because a marker can see the method and award it. An unexplained number cannot be given method marks, however correct it is.

Memory hook: Given, Find, Formula, Substitute. Every worked example in this book opens that way, so you will have copied the habit a hundred times before the exam.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Three words this course uses precisely
blocks.html:
Definition. A naming. It cannot be true or false, only used or misused. "n! means the product of every whole number from n down to 1" is a definition.

Theorem. A claim that has been proved. It is true, and something else depends on it. "There is no largest prime number" is a theorem: it is not a naming, it asserts something, and it has been established beyond doubt.

Proof. An argument that settles a claim for every case it covers. Checking three examples is not a proof, it is evidence. Part Nine builds proofs properly.

An exam that says "prove" and receives three examples gets the marks for three examples, which is usually zero.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. Translate "q is necessary for p" into symbols.

2. Translate "p only if q" into symbols.

3. A question says "determine whether 51 is prime". You write "No". How many of the 2 marks should you expect?

4. What is the difference between a definition and a theorem?

Answers

1. p → q. The necessary thing is the conclusion.
2. p → q. "Only if" also marks the conclusion.
3. About one, at best. "Determine whether" wants the verdict and the reason: exhibit what settles it, for instance "no, because 51 = 3 × 17".
4. A definition names something and cannot be true or false. A theorem makes a claim that has been proved true.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. "p is sufficient for q" in symbols is .
  2. "p if and only if q" in symbols is .
  3. An argument that settles a claim for every case is called a .
  4. The four-line answer runs Given, , Formula, .
Answers

1. p → q. 2. p ↔ q. 3. proof. 4. Find, Substitute.

title: Propositions and Truth Tables
lead:
Everything in this part is built from one idea: a sentence
  that is definitely true or definitely false, and nothing in between.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, answer the small question at the end of it, then slide the card down: the next frame opens with the answer. Do not read ahead. Being wrong here is the point.

frames.teach: A proposition is a sentence that is definitely true or definitely false, and never both. The world is round is one. Justice is not, and neither is Why is the sky blue.
frames.ask: Is the sentence Close the door a proposition?

frames.check: no. It is a command, so it is neither true nor false.
frames.teach: Conjunction is AND, and it is the strict one: true only when BOTH parts are true, so one row in four.
frames.ask: p is true and q is false. Is p AND q true?

frames.check: no. AND needs both.
frames.teach: Disjunction is OR, and it is the generous one: false only when BOTH parts fail, so three rows in four. It is the inclusive or, so both being true still counts.
frames.ask: p is true and q is true. Is p OR q true?

frames.check: yes. Inclusive or allows both.
frames.teach: Implication, p implies q, is false in exactly ONE row: p true and q false. Every other row is true, including the two where p is false.
frames.ask: It did not rain and you brought no umbrella. Did you break the promise if it rains I will bring an umbrella?

frames.check: no. It did not rain, so nothing was broken. That is why the implication is true.
frames.teach: Biconditional, p if and only if q, is true when both sides AGREE: both true, or both false. It is an equality test on truth values.
frames.ask: p false and q false. Is the biconditional true?

frames.check: yes. They agree.
frames.teach: So: AND needs both, OR needs one, IMPLIES fails only on true-then-false, and IF AND ONLY IF needs agreement. Four connectives, four one-line rules.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will be able to say whether a sentence is a proposition, write an English sentence in symbols, build a truth table for any compound proposition however tangled, and name a proposition as a tautology, a contradiction or a contingency.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both.

Three phrases in that definition are doing work. Declarative means it declares something, so it is not a question or a command. Either true or false means it has a definite truth value, even if nobody present knows which. Not both means it cannot be true in one breath and false in the next.

SentenceProposition?Why
Lagos is in Nigeria.Yes, trueIt declares something, and that something is the case.
2 + 2 = 5Yes, falseBeing false does not stop it being a proposition. It only needs a truth value.
What time is the exam?NoA question. It declares nothing, so there is nothing to be true.
Close the door.NoA command, for the same reason.
x + 1 = 3Not yetIts truth depends on x. Until x is fixed it has no truth value. Section 1.4 turns sentences like this into propositions.
This sentence is false.NoIf it is true it is false, and if it is false it is true. It breaks the "not both" rule.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both.

Propositions are written with letters, usually p, q, r, s. A letter standing for a proposition is a propositional variable. The two truth values are written T for true and F for false.

Memory hook: if you can sensibly answer "is that true?", it is a proposition. You cannot answer that about a question or an order.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Single propositions are not very interesting. We join them with connectives to make compound propositions, and the whole of this part is the study of how the truth of the pieces fixes the truth of the whole.

Each connective is defined by a truth table: a table listing every possible combination of truth values for the pieces, with the resulting value for the whole. A truth table is not an explanation of a connective, it is the connective. There is nothing more to know about "and" in logic than the four rows of its table.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
NameSymbolRead asTrue exactly when
Negation¬pnot pp is false
Conjunctionp ∧ qp and qboth are true
Disjunctionp ∨ qp or qat least one is true
Exclusive orp ⊕ qp or q but not bothexactly one is true
Implicationp → qif p then qp is false, or q is true
Biconditionalp ↔ qp if and only if qboth have the same truth value

Memory hook: ∧ points up like the A in "and"; ∨ is the other way up, for "or". → points from the assumption to the conclusion. ↔ points both ways because it works both ways.
Here are all six side by side. Learn to reproduce this from memory, because almost every logic question on every paper starts by using it.

pq¬pp ∧ qp ∨ qp ⊕ qp → qp ↔ q
TTFTTFTT
TFFFTTFF
FTTFTTTF
FFTFFFTT

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.tag: The row that costs marks every year
blocks.html:
Look at row 3 of p → q: p is false, q is true, and the implication is true. Now row 4: both false, and it is true again.

Students reject this because it feels wrong. "If I pass, I will celebrate" seems to say nothing about what happens when I fail. Exactly: it says nothing, and a promise that says nothing about a case has not been broken in that case. An implication is a promise, and a promise is false only when it is broken, which needs p true and q false.

p → q is false in exactly one case: p true, q false. Learn that as a single fact and the other three rows follow.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
English uses "or" in two ways. "Tea or coffee?" usually means one or the other but not both. "Applicants must have a degree or five years of experience" means at least one, and having both is fine.

Logic splits these. Disjunction (∨) is the inclusive one: true when at least one part is true, including when both are. Exclusive or (⊕) is the other: true when exactly one is true. Compare the rows where p and q are both true: ∨ gives T, ⊕ gives F. That single row is the whole difference.

blocks.text: Building a table for a compound proposition

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Any compound proposition, however tangled, is handled the same way.

Step 1. Count the letters. With n distinct propositional variables the table has 2n rows: 2 letters give 4 rows, 3 give 8, 4 give 16.

Step 2. Fill the letter columns mechanically. Under the first letter write T for the top half of the rows and F for the bottom half; under the next, alternate in blocks half that size; keep halving. Done this way you cannot miss a combination or write one twice.

Step 3. Work outward from the innermost bracket. Give every intermediate expression its own column. Do not jump to the final answer in one step: you cannot check a step you did not write down, and the marks are for the working.

Step 4. Read the final column. All T is a tautology, all F a contradiction, a mixture a contingency.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: Three names for a final column
blocks.html:
A compound proposition is a

tautology if it is true for every assignment of truth values, that is, the final column is all T;
contradiction if it is false for every assignment, all F;
contingency if it is neither, true for some assignments and false for others.

Memory hook: a tautology tells you nothing because it is always true, a contradiction is always false, and a contingency depends, which is what "contingent" means in ordinary English.
The 2020/2021 paper asks for the definitions and the tables together. Read what it actually says, including its own spelling.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
5. (a) Define and draw the truth table for each of the following logic proposition terminologies:

      
(i) Negation     (ii) Conjunction     (iii) Exclusive or     (iv) Implication

      
(v) Tautology     (vi) Contigency (6marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
The paper prints "Contigency". The word is contingency. Write the correct spelling in your answer; nobody has ever lost a mark for spelling the examiner's typo correctly. Notice too that (v) and (vi) are not connectives at all, so "draw the truth table for a tautology" does not quite make sense as written. What is wanted is an example whose table is all T, and one whose table is mixed.

Break it down
Given
Six terms: four connectives and two names for a shape of final column.
Asked
Two things for each. Define it in words, and draw its truth table. Half the marks are in the words, so a page of tables with no definitions scores about half.
Marks say
6 marks over six items is one mark each: one sentence and one small table apiece. Do not write an essay on implication.
Teaches
This section, 1.1.
Trap
Giving the table for ∨ when asked for exclusive or. They differ in exactly one row, and that row is the answer.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: (i) Negation. The negation of p, written ¬p, is the proposition "it is not the case that p". It reverses the truth value.

(ii) Conjunction. The conjunction of p and q, written p ∧ q, is "p and q". It is true only when both are true.

(iii) Exclusive or. The exclusive or of p and q, written p ⊕ q, is true when exactly one of them is true and false when they agree.

(iv) Implication. The implication p → q, read "if p then q", is false only when p is true and q is false. Here p is the hypothesis and q the conclusion.

(v) Tautology. A compound proposition that is true for every assignment of truth values to its variables. The standard example is p ∨ ¬p, "either it is raining or it is not".

For completeness, the third member of that family: a contradiction is false for every assignment, for example p ∧ ¬p.

blocks.redo: Now redo it: cover this answer and write out all six definitions and tables on blank paper. Time yourself; you should be inside six minutes.

blocks.text: A harder table, from the recent papers

blocks.html: The same skill on propositions with more structure. This one is worth quoting carefully, because part of it appears on two different papers.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
b. Construct a truth table for each of these compound propositions.

      
i.       p ↔ ¬p                     ii.       (q → ¬p) ↔ (p ↔ q)

      
iii.     (p ⊕ q) ∨ (p ⊕ ¬q)       iv.     ((p → q) → r) → s 4 marks

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(d) Construct a truth table for each of the following compound propositions

      
(i)  (p ↔ q) ⊖ (p ↔ ¬q) (5 marks)

      
(ii) (q → ¬p) ↔ (p ↔ q) (5 marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the 2021/2022 version
Part (i) prints the connective as ⊖, a circled minus. There is no standard logical connective with that symbol. In context it can only mean exclusive or, normally written ⊕, and the question is unanswerable on any other reading. Quote the glyph as printed, say in one line what it has to mean, and answer on that reading.

Note also that this paper prints "(5 marks)" with a space here, while every other mark on it is closed up as "5marks". Part (ii) is word for word the same proposition as 2024/2025 Q1 b(ii) above.

Note on the 2024/2025 version
Its part (ii) is word for word the 2021/2022 part (ii), so one table answers both papers and that one table is worth 5 marks on one paper and a share of 4 on the other. Note also that part (iv) has four letters, so its table needs 16 rows: four times the work of the others for the same share of the marks. In the hall, do i, ii and iii first.

Break it down
Given
Four compound propositions of increasing size: one letter, two, two, then four.
Asked
Construct a truth table. Not "simplify", not "say whether it is a tautology". Build the table; any conclusion you then draw from it is a bonus that shows you understood it.
Marks say
4 marks for four tables is one mark each, and one of them is 16 rows. So the marks are for method, not endurance: set the columns out cleanly and the mark is yours.
Teaches
This section, 1.1, plus 1.3 for the shortcut on (ii).
Trap
Rushing (iv) and losing a row. Fill the letter columns by halving, as in Step 2, and you cannot go wrong.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: (i) p ↔ ¬p. One letter, so 2 rows. The biconditional is true when both sides agree, and p never agrees with ¬p.
blocks.working:
p¬pp ↔ ¬p
TFF
FTF

Every row is F, so p ↔ ¬p is a contradiction. Say so: naming it shows you understood the table you just drew.

(ii) (q → ¬p) ↔ (p ↔ q). Two letters, so 4 rows. Build the pieces first: ¬p, then q → ¬p, then p ↔ q, then join them.

pq¬pq → ¬pp ↔ qwhole
TTFFTF
TFFTFF
FTTTFF
FFTTTT

Taking the rows one at a time, remembering that → is false only for T then F, and ↔ is true only when its two sides match:

Row 1: q is T and ¬p is F, so q → ¬p is F. p ↔ q with both T is T. F against T gives F.
Row 2: q is F, so q → ¬p is T whatever follows it. p ↔ q with T and F is F. T against F gives F.
Row 3: q is T and ¬p is T, so T. p ↔ q with F and T is F. T against F gives F.
Row 4: q is F so the implication is T. p ↔ q with both F is T. T against T gives T.

Three F rows and one T row, so this is a contingency. It is true exactly when p and q are both false.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: parts (iii) and (iv) are yours. For (iii) expect a surprise in the final column, and say what it means. For (iv) remember 16 rows, and fill the p column as 8 T then 8 F.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. In which single case is p → q false?

2. How many rows does a truth table with 5 letters have?

3. In which row do p ∨ q and p ⊕ q disagree?

4. Is "x > 3" a proposition?

Answers

1. When p is true and q is false, and in no other.
2. 25 = 32.
3. When both are true: ∨ gives T, ⊕ gives F.
4. No. Its truth depends on x, so it has no truth value until x is fixed. It is a predicate, and Section 1.4 shows how to turn it into a proposition.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. A declarative sentence that is either true or false but not both is called a .
  2. The connective ∧ is called and is true only when parts are true.
  3. A compound proposition whose final column is entirely T is a , entirely F a , and mixed a .
  4. With n distinct variables a truth table has rows.
Answers

1. proposition. 2. conjunction, both. 3. tautology, contradiction, contingency. 4. 2n.

blocks.label: Every test question on propositional logic

title: Implication, Converse, Inverse, Contrapositive
lead:
One implication has three relatives. Exactly one of them says
  the same thing as the original, and every paper in our set asks you which.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, answer the small question at the end of it, then slide the card down: the next frame opens with the answer. Do not read ahead. Being wrong here is the point.

frames.teach: From p implies q you can build three related statements, and the exam asks you to name them. The converse swaps the two: q implies p.
frames.ask: The converse of if it rains then the ground is wet?

frames.check: if the ground is wet then it rained. Which need not be true: somebody may have washed the car.
frames.teach: The inverse negates both without swapping: not-p implies not-q.
frames.ask: The inverse of the same statement?

frames.check: if it does not rain then the ground is not wet. Also not guaranteed.
frames.teach: The contrapositive does both: swap AND negate, giving not-q implies not-p.
frames.ask: Which of the three is logically the SAME as the original?

frames.check: the contrapositive. That is why proving it proves the original.
frames.teach: So converse and inverse may be false when the original is true, and they are equivalent to each other. Contrapositive is the only safe one.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will be able to form the converse, inverse and contrapositive of any conditional statement, in English or in symbols, and prove which one preserves truth value.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Start with a conditional statement p → q. There are exactly three ways to rearrange it, and each has a name.

The converse swaps the two parts: q → p.

The inverse negates both parts, keeping the order: ¬p → ¬q.

The contrapositive does both, swap and negate: ¬q → ¬p.

Watch what happens to a concrete case. Let p be "it is a dog" and q "it is an animal", so p → q reads "if it is a dog then it is an animal", which is true.

NameFormThe dog exampleTrue?
Originalp → qIf it is a dog, it is an animal.yes
Converseq → pIf it is an animal, it is a dog.no, a cat is a counterexample
Inverse¬p → ¬qIf it is not a dog, it is not an animal.no, the same cat
Contrapositive¬q → ¬pIf it is not an animal, it is not a dog.yes

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
For any conditional statement p → q:

converse = q → p
inverse = ¬p → ¬q
contrapositive = ¬q → ¬p

Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original. The converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other, and neither follows from the original.

Memory hook: Converse Changes order. Inverse Inverts (negates) both. Contrapositive does both, and doing both is the only safe operation. In the dog example: knowing it is not an animal really does tell you it is not a dog.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Proving it rather than asserting it
blocks.html:
The 2024/2025 paper does not ask you to state this, it asks you to prove it, for six marks. A truth table is the proof.

pq¬p¬qp → qq → p¬p → ¬q¬q → ¬p
TTFFTTTT
TFFTFTTF
FTTFTFFT
FFTTTTTT

Read the columns, not the rows. The column for p → q is T, F, T, T. The column for the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p is T, F, T, T: identical, so they are equivalent.

The converse column is T, T, F, T and the inverse column is T, T, F, T: identical to each other, and different from the original in rows 2 and 3. So the converse and inverse are equivalent to each other and neither is equivalent to p → q. That single table proves every claim in this section at once.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
c. Consider the conditional statement:

      
"The home team wins whenever it is raining."

      
Let p represent: "It is raining."

      
Let q represent: "The home team wins."

      
i.       Using this, find the following: the contrapositive, the converse, and the inverse of the statement. 3 marks

      
ii.       Prove that only the contrapositive of a conditional statement p → q has the same truth value as the original conditional statement. Use the statement from c(i) in your explanation. 6 marks

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
The paper hands you the letters, which is a gift: p is the rain, not the win. Read that assignment twice before writing, because the sentence puts the win first and the rain second, while the letters run the other way.

Break it down
Given
The sentence "The home team wins whenever it is raining.", with p = it is raining and q = the home team wins.
Asked
Part i: find three rearrangements, in English. Part ii: prove a general claim, then illustrate it with this sentence. "Prove" means a truth table or a full argument, not an assertion.
Marks say
3 marks for three statements is one each, so short English sentences suffice. 6 marks for the proof is the bulk of the question: that is a full table with the columns compared and a conclusion written out.
Teaches
This section, 1.2, and 1.1 for the table method.
Trap
"Whenever" marks the hypothesis, so the statement is p → q (rain implies win), not q → p. Getting that backwards inverts all three answers in part i and costs the lot.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
p = "It is raining", q = "The home team wins", and the sentence "The home team wins whenever it is raining."
Find
The contrapositive, converse and inverse, then a proof that only the contrapositive preserves truth value.
Rule
converse q → p, inverse ¬p → ¬q, contrapositive ¬q → ¬p.

Step 1. Get the direction right. "The home team wins whenever it is raining" rewrites as "if it is raining, then the home team wins". So the statement is p → q.

Step 2 (part i). Apply each definition.

NameSymbolsIn English
Contrapositive¬q → ¬pIf the home team does not win, then it is not raining.
Converseq → pIf the home team wins, then it is raining.
Inverse¬p → ¬qIf it is not raining, then the home team does not win.

Step 3 (part ii). Prove it with a truth table. Build every column and compare them against p → q.

pq¬p¬qp → q¬q → ¬pq → p¬p → ¬q
TTFFTTTT
TFFTFFTT
FTTFTTFF
FFTTTTTT

The p → q column reads T, F, T, T. The contrapositive column reads T, F, T, T. They agree in every row, so p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p. The converse reads T, T, F, T and disagrees with the original in rows 2 and 3, and the inverse matches the converse rather than the original.

Step 4. Say it in words, using their sentence. Suppose it rains and the home team loses. That single situation makes the original false, because the promise was broken. It also makes the contrapositive false: the team did not win, yet it was raining. The two statements fail together and hold together, which is what equivalence means.

Now the converse. Suppose the home team wins on a dry day. The original is untouched, since it only ever promised something about rainy days, so it stays true. But the converse, "if the home team wins then it is raining", is false. One statement true, the other false, so they are not equivalent. The inverse fails on that same dry, winning day.

Conclusion. Of the three rearrangements only the contrapositive always carries the same truth value as the original.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: cover this and do the whole question for "I go to the beach whenever it is a sunny summer day", which is 2024/2025 Q1(a)(ii).

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
a.       State the converse, contrapositive, and inverse of each of these conditional statements.

      
i. If it snows tonight, then I will stay at home.

      
ii. I go to the beach whenever it is a sunny summer day.

      
iii. When I stay up late, it is necessary that I sleep until noon. 4.5 marks

blocks.html:
Break it down
Given
Three English sentences, each hiding an implication in a different disguise: a plain "if ... then", a "whenever", and a "necessary that".
Asked
State three rearrangements of each, so nine sentences in all. English is fine; symbols are not required but help you avoid errors.
Marks say
4.5 marks over nine statements is half a mark each. Write them as short sentences and move on; there are no marks for commentary here.
Teaches
This section for the three forms, F.2 for decoding "whenever" and "necessary".
Trap
All three sentences put the pieces in a different order from p → q. Identify p and q explicitly, in the margin, before writing a single answer.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem:
(i) "If it snows tonight, then I will stay at home."
Already in standard form. p = it snows tonight, q = I will stay at home.
blocks.working:
Converse: If I stay at home tonight, then it will snow.
Inverse: If it does not snow tonight, then I will not stay at home.
Contrapositive: If I do not stay at home tonight, then it will not snow.

(ii) "I go to the beach whenever it is a sunny summer day."
"Whenever" marks the hypothesis. p = it is a sunny summer day, q = I go to the beach. Rewritten: if it is a sunny summer day, then I go to the beach.

Converse: If I go to the beach, then it is a sunny summer day.
Inverse: If it is not a sunny summer day, then I do not go to the beach.
Contrapositive: If I do not go to the beach, then it is not a sunny summer day.

(iii) "When I stay up late, it is necessary that I sleep until noon."
"When" marks the hypothesis and "it is necessary that" marks the conclusion. p = I stay up late, q = I sleep until noon. Rewritten: if I stay up late, then I sleep until noon.

Converse: If I sleep until noon, then I stayed up late.
Inverse: If I do not stay up late, then I do not sleep until noon.
Contrapositive: If I do not sleep until noon, then I did not stay up late.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: nine sentences, blank paper, four minutes. If any of yours reverses the roles of p and q, go back to F.2 and re-read the phrase table.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
The negation of "I will stay at home" is "I will not stay at home". It is not "I will go out", however natural that sounds. Staying at home and going out might not exhaust the possibilities, and logic only knows what you wrote down.

Similarly, the negation of "x > 3" is "x ≤ 3", not "x < 3". Dropping the equality case is the commonest numeric slip on this topic.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. Which one of the three relatives is equivalent to the original?

2. Write the contrapositive of "if n is even then n² is even".

3. The converse is equivalent to which other statement?

4. What is the negation of "x ≥ 5"?

Answers

1. The contrapositive.
2. If n² is not even, then n is not even.
3. The inverse. Both are T, T, F, T.
4. x < 5.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. The converse of p → q is .
  2. The inverse of p → q is .
  3. The contrapositive of p → q is .
  4. Only the has the same truth value as the original.
Answers

1. q → p. 2. ¬p → ¬q. 3. ¬q → ¬p. 4. contrapositive.

title: Logical Equivalence and the Laws
lead:
Two statements that always agree can be swapped freely. That is
  what lets you simplify a condition, redesign a circuit, or rewrite a database
  query without changing what it does.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, answer the small question at the end of it, then slide the card down: the next frame opens with the answer. Do not read ahead. Being wrong here is the point.

frames.teach: Two statements are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row of the truth table. The biconditional is the test.
frames.ask: How would you prove two expressions equivalent using a truth table?

frames.check: build both columns and check they agree in every row.
frames.teach: De Morgan's laws are the pair worth knowing cold: not (p AND q) is not-p OR not-q, and not (p OR q) is not-p AND not-q.
frames.ask: Negate it is raining AND cold.

frames.check: it is not raining OR it is not cold. The AND flips to OR.
frames.teach: The one that shortens most proofs: p implies q is equivalent to not-p OR q. Every implication can be rewritten without an arrow.
frames.ask: Rewrite if it rains then I stay in, using OR.

frames.check: it does not rain, or I stay in.
frames.teach: A tautology is true in every row, a contradiction false in every row, and a contingency is neither.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will be able to test two propositions for equivalence with a truth table, state De Morgan's laws properly as laws, and use the standard laws to transform one expression into another.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Two compound propositions are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value for every possible assignment of truth values to their variables. We write P ≡ Q.

Equivalently: P ≡ Q exactly when the biconditional P ↔ Q is a tautology.

Memory hook: ≡ is the equals sign with an extra bar, meaning "equal in every row, not just this one". It is a claim about two propositions, so it is not itself a connective.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: How to show two things are equivalent
blocks.html:
There are two accepted methods, and the question usually tells you which it wants.

Method 1: truth table. Build a column for each side and check they match row for row. Always works, never elegant, and cannot fail through a wrong step. Use it when the question says "show that" or "construct a truth table".

Method 2: a chain of known laws. Rewrite one side step by step until it becomes the other, naming the law at every step. Shorter when it works, and it is what "using logical equivalences" means when a paper says so, as 2024/2025 Q3(c) does.

The naming is not decoration. In a law-chain proof the marks are for the justifications, so a chain of correct lines with no names attached scores poorly.

De Morgan's laws

The claim. Negating a conjunction turns it into the disjunction of the negations, and negating a disjunction turns it into the conjunction of the negations. In words: not (both) is the same as (not one) or (not the other), and not (either) is the same as (not one) and (not the other).

In symbols.
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q

Conditions. None beyond p and q being propositions. The laws hold universally, which is what makes them safe to apply anywhere.

The limiting case, and why the wrong version survives. The common error is to write ¬(p ∧ q) as ¬p ∧ ¬q, keeping the connective instead of flipping it. Those two agree in exactly the rows where p and q have the same truth value, and differ in the other two. So a student who checks only the TT and FF rows sees the wrong law confirmed. Check a row where p and q disagree, and the error appears at once.

The same laws for sets. Replacing "and" by intersection, "or" by union and "not" by complement gives the set forms, which Part Two uses:
the complement of (A ∩ B) = (complement of A) ∪ (complement of B)
the complement of (A ∪ B) = (complement of A) ∩ (complement of B)

Consequence. A negation can always be pushed inwards until it sits on single variables. That is why every Boolean expression can be simplified mechanically, and why a compiler can rewrite your if conditions.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Say it about breakfast. "It is not the case that I had both tea and toast" means "I did not have tea, or I did not have toast" (at least one of them was missing). It does not mean I had neither.

"It is not the case that I had either tea or toast" is the stronger one: it means I had no tea and no toast.

So negation flips the connective as it moves inside. Forgetting to flip it is the mistake De Morgan exists to prevent.

pqp ∧ q¬(p ∧ q)¬p¬q¬p ∨ ¬q
TTTFFFF
TFFTFTT
FTFTTFT
FFFTTTT

Columns four and seven are both F, T, T, T. The law is proved.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Here T means a tautology (always true) and F a contradiction (always false).

NameLaw
Identityp ∧ T ≡ p     p ∨ F ≡ p
Dominationp ∨ T ≡ T     p ∧ F ≡ F
Idempotentp ∨ p ≡ p     p ∧ p ≡ p
Double negation¬(¬p) ≡ p
Commutativep ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p     p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p
Associative(p ∨ q) ∨ r ≡ p ∨ (q ∨ r)
Distributivep ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r)
De Morgan¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q     ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q
Absorptionp ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p     p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p
Negationp ∨ ¬p ≡ T     p ∧ ¬p ≡ F
Implicationp → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
Contrapositivep → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p
Biconditionalp ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)

Memory hook: the one that unlocks most problems is implication: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q. An arrow is hard to manipulate; an "or" is easy. Turn every arrow into an or as your first move, and most chains fall out.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(c) Show that the following are logically equivalent

      
(i) (p → q) ∧ (p → r) and p → (q ∧ r). (3marks)

      
(ii) p ↔ q and (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q) (3marks)

blocks.html:
Break it down
Given
Two pairs of compound propositions, the first on three letters and the second on two.
Asked
Show that each pair is equivalent. A truth table is a complete answer, and is safer than a law chain under time pressure.
Marks say
3 marks each. Part (i) has three letters so its table is 8 rows; part (ii) has two letters and 4 rows. Both are quick if the columns are set out before you start filling.
Teaches
This section for equivalence, 1.1 for building the table.
Trap
Part (i) needs 8 rows, and the temptation is to do 4. Count the distinct letters, not the brackets.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
(p → q) ∧ (p → r) and p → (q ∧ r).
Find
Whether the two columns agree in every row.
Rule
Three letters, so 2³ = 8 rows.
pqrp→qp→r(p→q)∧(p→r)q∧rp→(q∧r)
TTTTTTTT
TTFTFFFF
TFTFTFFF
TFFFFFFF
FTTTTTTT
FTFTTTFT
FFTTTTFT
FFFTTTFT

Column 6 reads T, F, F, F, T, T, T, T. Column 8 reads T, F, F, F, T, T, T, T. Identical in all eight rows, so (p → q) ∧ (p → r) ≡ p → (q ∧ r).

Sanity check in words: promising q and promising r separately, on the same condition p, is the same as promising both together on that condition. It should feel obvious, and the table is why it is certain.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
p ↔ q and (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q).
Find
Whether the two agree in every row.
Rule
Two letters, 4 rows.
pqp↔qp∧q¬p¬q¬p∧¬q(p∧q)∨(¬p∧¬q)
TTTTFFFT
TFFFFTFF
FTFFTFFF
FFTFTTTT

Column 3 is T, F, F, T and column 8 is T, F, F, T. Equivalent.

In words: "p and q agree" is the same as "either both are true, or both are false". That is exactly what the biconditional means, so the right-hand side is really the definition written out.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: on blank paper, show that p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q with a truth table. It is the law you will lean on most.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
Equivalence needs agreement in every row. Two propositions that match in three rows out of four are not "nearly equivalent", they are simply different, and the one row where they differ is the counterexample you should quote.

When a question asks you to show two things are not equivalent, do not build the whole table and say "they differ". Name the row: "take p true and q false; then the first is F and the second is T". One row, fully specified, is a complete disproof.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. State both of De Morgan's laws.

2. Rewrite p → q without using the arrow.

3. Simplify p ∨ (p ∧ q).

4. How many rows are needed to test an equivalence on four letters?

Answers

1. ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q.
2. ¬p ∨ q.
3. p, by the absorption law.
4. 2⁴ = 16.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. P ≡ Q means the two have the same truth value for assignment.
  2. ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ .
  3. The implication law says p → q ≡ .
  4. p ∧ ¬p ≡ .
Answers

1. every. 2. ¬p ∧ ¬q. 3. ¬p ∨ q. 4. F (a contradiction).

title: Predicate Logic and Quantifiers
lead:
Propositional logic cannot say "every student has a laptop"
  without inventing a letter for each student. Predicate logic can, and that is
  the whole reason it exists.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, answer the small question at the end of it, then slide the card down: the next frame opens with the answer. Do not read ahead. Being wrong here is the point.

frames.teach: A predicate is a sentence with a variable in it, such as P(x): x is greater than 3. It is neither true nor false until you do something to the variable.
frames.ask: Is P(x): x is greater than 3 true or false?

frames.check: neither, until x is given a value.
frames.teach: There are two ways to settle it. The first is to substitute: P(5) is true, P(1) is false. That turns a predicate into a proposition.
frames.ask: What is the other way to turn a predicate into a proposition?

frames.check: quantify it: for all x, or there exists an x.
frames.teach: The truth set of a predicate is the collection of values from the domain that make it TRUE. For P(x): x is greater than 3 over the naturals, that is 4, 5, 6 and onwards.
frames.ask: What is the truth set of x squared equals 4 over the integers?

frames.check: the set containing 2 and minus 2.
frames.teach: The universal quantifier, for all, needs EVERY case to hold. A single counterexample destroys it.
frames.ask: For all natural numbers n, n is greater than 3. True or false?

frames.check: false. n equals 1 is a counterexample.
frames.teach: The existential quantifier, there exists, needs only ONE case. One example proves it.
frames.ask: Which symbol is the backwards E, and what does it mean?

frames.check: the existential one, meaning there exists.
frames.teach: Backwards E for Exists, upside-down A for All. Universal needs everything and dies to one counterexample; existential needs one thing and lives on one example.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will be able to say exactly how predicate logic differs from propositional logic, use both quantifiers correctly, translate an English sentence with "some", "all", "no" or "every" into symbols, negate a quantified statement, and decide the truth of a quantified statement over the real numbers.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
In Part One so far, p was an entire sentence with a fixed truth value. That is fine for "it is raining", but it cannot see inside a sentence.

Consider "every student in this class has a laptop". With propositional letters you would need one letter per student, and you would still have no way to say "every". Worse, "x + 1 = 3" cannot be a proposition at all, because its truth depends on x.

Predicate logic fixes both problems by splitting a sentence into a subject and a property, and then adding words for "all" and "some".

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
A predicate is a statement containing one or more variables, which becomes a proposition once the variables are given values. We write P(x), read "P of x".

If P(x) is "x > 3", then P(5) is "5 > 3", which is true, and P(1) is "1 > 3", which is false. P(x) on its own is neither.

AxisPropositional logicPredicate logic
Smallest unita whole sentence, pa predicate with variables, P(x)
Can see inside a sentencenoyes, subject and property are separate
Quantifiersnone∀ and ∃
Can express "all" and "some"noyes
Examplep = "Ada has a laptop"L(x) = "x has a laptop", so ∀x L(x)

Memory hook: propositional logic treats a sentence as a sealed box. Predicate logic opens the box and finds a subject and a property inside.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
The universal quantifier ∀, read "for all" or "for every". ∀x P(x) is true exactly when P(x) is true for every x in the domain.

The existential quantifier ∃, read "there exists" or "for some". ∃x P(x) is true exactly when P(x) is true for at least one x in the domain.

The domain (or universe of discourse) is the collection the variable ranges over. It must always be stated, because the same statement can flip truth value when the domain changes.

∀ universal∃ existential
Read asfor all, for every, for eachthere exists, for some, at least one
True whenevery element satisfies Pat least one element satisfies P
False whenone counterexample existsevery element fails P
To prove ita general argument covering all casesproduce one witness
To disprove itproduce one counterexamplea general argument that none works
Pairs with→ usually∧ usually

Memory hook: ∀ is an upside-down A for All. ∃ is a back-to-front E for Exists. The asymmetry in the last two rows is worth learning on its own: one example kills a "for all" and one example makes a "there exists".

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.tag: ∀ takes an arrow, ∃ takes an and
blocks.html:
This is the single most common error in translation, and it appears on every paper that asks for one.

"Every student in the class has a laptop" is ∀x (S(x) → L(x)), with an arrow. Writing ∀x (S(x) ∧ L(x)) instead would claim that everything in the universe is a student and has a laptop, which is far stronger and almost certainly false.

"Some student has a laptop" is ∃x (S(x) ∧ L(x)), with an and. Writing ∃x (S(x) → L(x)) instead is nearly useless: it is satisfied by any non-student at all, since a false hypothesis makes the implication true.

If the domain is already restricted to students, the qualifier disappears and you write ∀x L(x) or ∃x L(x). Say which domain you are using.

De Morgan's laws for quantifiers

The claim. A negation moved across a quantifier flips it. Saying "not everything has the property" is the same as saying "something lacks it", and saying "nothing has the property" is the same as saying "everything lacks it".

In symbols.
¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)
¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x)

Conditions. None. They hold for any predicate over any domain.

The limiting case. Over a finite domain {a1, …, an}, ∀ is a chain of conjunctions and ∃ a chain of disjunctions, so these two laws collapse into the propositional De Morgan laws of section 1.3 applied n times. They are not a second pair of laws but the same pair, stretched over a domain. Over an empty domain they still hold, and the check is worth doing once: ∀x P(x) is true there (nothing fails) and ∃x P(x) is false (nothing succeeds), so both sides of the first law come out false.

Consequence. Any negation can be pushed inwards until it rests on a bare predicate, flipping every quantifier it passes. This is how "no student has a cat, a dog and a ferret" gets written two different but equivalent ways, which 2024/2025 Q2(a)(iv) exploits.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
"Not all swans are white" means "some swan is not white". You have not claimed all swans are non-white, only that at least one is.

"No swan is green" means "every swan is not green". Here the negation does apply to all of them.

Notice that "no" is a negated existential: "no x has property P" is ¬∃x P(x), which becomes ∀x ¬P(x). Whenever an exam sentence starts with "No", write it as a negated "there exists" first, then convert if you want.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
a.       Let C(x) be the statement "x has a cat," let D(x) be the statement "x has a dog," and let F (x) be the statement "x has a ferret."
