By contrast f(x) = x² on the reals has no inverse: it is neither one-to-one nor onto, and "the square root" cannot decide between 2 and −2.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. In f ∘ g, which function acts first?

2. With f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 3x, find both compositions.

3. What must be true of f for f−1 to exist?

4. Is composition commutative?

Answers

1. g, the one written nearest x.
2. (f ∘ g)(x) = 3x + 1 and (g ∘ f)(x) = 3(x + 1) = 3x + 3.
3. f must be a bijection: one-to-one and onto.
4. No. f ∘ g and g ∘ f generally differ.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. (f ∘ g)(x) means .
  2. Composition is read from to .
  3. An inverse exists exactly when the function is a .
  4. For f(x) = x² + 1 and g(x) = x + 2, (f ∘ g)(x) = .
Answers

1. f(g(x)). 2. right, left. 3. bijection. 4. x² + 4x + 5.

title: Sequences, Series and Progressions
lead:
A sequence is an ordered list with a rule behind it. Two rules
  cover almost everything this course does with them: keep adding the same
  amount, or keep multiplying by the same amount. Getting the indexing right is
  where the marks actually go.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, answer the small question at the end of it, then slide the card down: the next frame opens with the answer. Do not read ahead. Being wrong here is the point.

frames.teach: A sequence is formally a FUNCTION whose domain is a subset of the integers, usually 1, 2, 3 onwards. The third term is that function's value at 3.
frames.ask: Does order matter in a sequence?

frames.check: yes. The input decides the position.
frames.teach: An arithmetic progression ADDS a fixed common difference d. Find d by SUBTRACTING consecutive terms.
frames.ask: 2, 4, 6, 8. What is d?

frames.teach: A geometric progression MULTIPLIES by a fixed common ratio r. Find r by DIVIDING consecutive terms.
Their nth terms follow from that. AP: a plus (n minus 1)d. GP: a times r to the power n minus 1.
frames.ask: Test any sequence how? Say the method in one line.

frames.check: subtract for a common difference, divide for a common ratio, and whichever comes out constant names it.
frames.teach: Fibonacci is neither: each term is the SUM OF THE TWO BEFORE IT, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. That makes it a recurrence rather than a progression.
frames.ask: A sequence with a fixed number of terms is called what?

frames.check: a finite sequence.
frames.teach: Add for arithmetic, multiply for geometric, add the previous two for Fibonacci.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will be able to define a sequence and a term, tell an arithmetic progression from a geometric one, write the general term and the sum of each, read a rule off a printed sequence, use sigma notation and the four standard sums, and state which indexing convention you are using so that an off-by-one cannot cost you.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
A sequence is a function from a subset of the integers, usually {0, 1, 2, …} or {1, 2, 3, …}, to a set S. The image of the integer n is written an and is called a term of the sequence. The whole sequence is written {an}.

Where n is the index, an integer, and it says the position of the term, not its value. an is the term at position n: one number, not the whole list. The subscript is not multiplication. {an} in braces is the sequence itself, the entire ordered list. S is the set the terms are drawn from, usually the real numbers on this course.

Calling it a function is the useful part. Section 4.1 defined a function as a rule assigning exactly one output to each input; a sequence is that rule with the inputs restricted to integers. So each position has exactly one term, which is why "the third term" is a well-formed phrase.

Finite and infinite. A finite sequence has a last term and its length is the number of terms. An infinite sequence runs on without end.

SequenceKindThe rule behind it
2, 4, 6, 8, …, 20finite, length 10add 2 to the previous term
10, 6, 2, −2, …infinitesubtract 4 from the previous term
1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …infiniteadd the previous two terms

A progression is a sequence whose terms can be described by a formula. The third row above is the Fibonacci sequence, in which each term is the sum of the two before it; section 9.4 solves it properly.

Memory hook: the index is the seat number, the term is who is sitting in it.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
An arithmetic progression is a sequence in which each term is the previous term plus a fixed amount:

a,   a + d,   a + 2d,   a + 3d,   …

The general term and the sum of the first n terms are

an = a + (n − 1)d     and     Sn = n(a + an) / 2 = n(2a + (n − 1)d) / 2

Where a is the first term, the one at position 1. d is the common difference, the fixed amount added each time; it may be negative, which makes the sequence decrease, and it is found as any term minus the one before it. n is the position of the term you want, counting the first term as position 1. an is the n-th term. Sn is the sum of the first n terms, also called the arithmetic series. (n − 1) is the number of steps taken to get from the first term to the n-th, which is one fewer than the number of terms. That subtraction is the single most common error in this topic.

Why the sum formula looks like that. Write the sum forwards and backwards under itself and add column by column. Each column gives a + an, and there are n columns, so twice the sum is n(a + an). It is the first term plus the last, times how many pairs there are. The n = 1 to 100 case of section 9.2 is exactly this trick.

Memory hook: arithmetic adds, and the n-th term has taken n minus one steps.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
The definition above starts counting at 1, so a1 = a and an = a + (n − 1)d. The official course text writes the same progression as

a,   a + d,   a + 2d,   …,   a + nd

which counts from 0, so that its an = a + nd and its first term is a0. Neither is wrong. They describe the same list of numbers and disagree only about what to call the positions.

The danger is mixing them inside one answer, which produces an answer exactly one term out. So do two things:

  • Say which you are using, in five words: "counting the first term as a1".
  • Answer the question in the words it asked. "Find the 10th term" means the tenth number in the list, whatever you have chosen to call its index. Count the list if you are unsure; ten numbers is not many.

This is the same discipline as the Foundations convention box on whether ℕ contains 0, and for the same reason: a stated convention cannot be marked wrong.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
The sequence 7, 12, 17, 22, …
Find
(a) the 10th term, (b) a general formula for the n-th term, and (c) the sum of the first 10 terms.
Formula
an = a + (n − 1)d and Sn = n(a + an) / 2, counting the first term as a1.

Identify it first. The differences are 12 − 7 = 5, 17 − 12 = 5, 22 − 17 = 5. Constant, so this is an arithmetic progression with a = 7 and d = 5.

(a) The 10th term

a10 = a + (10 − 1)d = 7 + 9 × 5 = 7 + 45 = 52

Check by listing, which is cheap and catches an off-by-one at once: 7, 12, 17, 22, 27, 32, 37, 42, 47, 52. Ten numbers, and the tenth is 52.

(b) The general term

an = 7 + (n − 1) × 5 = 7 + 5n − 5 = 5n + 2

Test it at both ends: n = 1 gives 7, and n = 10 gives 50 + 2 = 52. Both agree.

(c) The sum of the first 10 terms

S10 = 10 × (7 + 52) / 2 = 10 × 59 / 2 = 295
blocks.redo: Now redo it: for 2, 4, 6, …, 20, we have a = 2, d = 2 and 10 terms, so the sum is 10 × (2 + 20) / 2 = 110 .

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
A geometric progression is a sequence in which each term is the previous term times a fixed amount:

a,   ar,   ar2,   ar3,   …

The general term and the sum of the first n terms are

an = arn−1     and     Sn = a(rn − 1) / (r − 1)   for r ≠ 1

Where a is the first term. r is the common ratio, the fixed multiplier, found as any term divided by the one before it. It may be a fraction, which makes the terms shrink, and it may be negative, which makes the signs alternate. n − 1 is again the number of multiplications performed to reach position n from position 1. r ≠ 1 is required because at r = 1 the formula divides by zero; that case is just n copies of a, so Sn = na.

The infinite sum. If the ratio is small enough that the terms shrink, that is if r lies strictly between −1 and 1, the infinite series has a finite total:

S = a / (1 − r)

Outside that range the terms do not shrink and the sum has no finite value.

Memory hook: arithmetic adds d, geometric times by r. To tell which one a printed sequence is: take differences, and if they are not constant, take ratios.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.tag: Method · reading a rule off a sequence
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
(a) 4, 8, 16, 32, …   (b) 1, 1/3, 1/9, 1/27, …   (c) 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, …
Find
The rule and the general term of each, plus one sum.
Formula
Differences first; if they are not constant, ratios. Then an = a + (n − 1)d or an = arn−1.

(a) 4, 8, 16, 32

Differences are 4, 8, 16: not constant. Ratios are 8 / 4 = 2, 16 / 8 = 2, 32 / 16 = 2: constant. So it is geometric with a = 4 and r = 2, and

an = 4 × 2n−1

A neater equivalent form, worth writing beside it: 4 × 2n−1 = 22 × 2n−1 = 2n+1. Check at n = 1: 22 = 4. At n = 4: 25 = 32.

The 10th term is 211 = 2048, and the sum of the first 10 terms is

S10 = 4(210 − 1) / (2 − 1) = 4 × 1023 = 4092

(b) 1, 1/3, 1/9, 1/27

The denominators are powers of 3, so the ratio is 1/3 and the first term is 1:

an = (1/3)n−1

Here the infinite sum exists, because 1/3 lies between −1 and 1:

S = a / (1 − r) = 1 / (1 − 1/3) = 1 / (2/3) = 3/2

So adding infinitely many terms gives 1.5 exactly, not something unbounded. That is worth one sentence of comment in an exam, because it is the point of the formula.

(c) 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

Differences are all 2, so it is arithmetic with a = 1, d = 2, and

an = 1 + (n − 1) × 2 = 2n − 1

which is the sequence of odd numbers, exactly the one section 9.2 summed to n2.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.tag: Method · when neither differences nor ratios are constant
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
The sequence 1, 5, 17, 53, 161, 485.
Find
The rule that generates it.
Formula
None applies directly: the two standard tests, a constant difference and a constant ratio, both fail, so the rule has to be found by comparing each term with the one before it.

Find the rule behind 1, 5, 17, 53, 161, 485.

Differences: 4, 12, 36, 108, 324. Not constant, so it is not arithmetic. Ratios: 5, 3.4, about 3.12, about 3.04, about 3.01. Not constant, so it is not geometric either. But the ratios are creeping towards 3, which is the hint.

Try "times 3 plus something".

Term3 × previousActualDifference
a23 × 1 = 352
a33 × 5 = 15172
a43 × 17 = 51532
a53 × 53 = 1591612
a63 × 161 = 4834852

The extra is 2 every time, so the rule is

an = 3an−1 + 2,   with   a1 = 1

That is a recurrence relation, a rule that defines each term from earlier ones rather than from n directly. Section 9.4 takes this exact sequence and produces a closed formula for an that needs no earlier terms at all.

The general procedure, when a sequence resists both standard shapes:

  1. Take differences. Constant means arithmetic.
  2. Take ratios. Constant means geometric.
  3. Take second differences. Constant means the terms follow a quadratic in n.
  4. Compare each term with a multiple of its predecessor. A constant leftover means a recurrence of the form an = can−1 + b.
  5. Try the sum of the previous two. That is Fibonacci.

blocks.text: Sigma notation and the standard sums

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: Four sums worth knowing by heart
blocks.html:
Summation notation was introduced in Foundations; here are the four closed forms this course expects, each valid for n ≥ 1.

SumClosed formCheck at n = 5
1 + 2 + … + nn(n + 1) / 25 × 6 / 2 = 15
12 + 22 + … + n2n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 65 × 6 × 11 / 6 = 55
13 + 23 + … + n3(n(n + 1) / 2)2152 = 225
1 + r + r2 + … + rn(rn+1 − 1) / (r − 1)at r = 2: 26 − 1 = 63
Where ∑ is the summation sign: the letter below it is the index, the value below it is where the index starts, the value above it is where it stops, and the expression after it is what to add. n is the last index, so these sums have n terms when they start at 1 and n + 1 terms when they start at 0. The geometric row starts at r0 = 1, which is why its exponent is n + 1. r is the common ratio as above, and r ≠ 1.

The third one is the square of the first, which is a memorable accident worth using: the sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n numbers.

Two rules that let you take a sum apart, and they are used constantly:

∑ (xk + yk) = ∑ xk + ∑ yk
∑ c xk = c ∑ xk, for a constant c

Memory hook: squares over six, cubes are the square of the first sum. And every one of these four can be proved by induction, which is section 9.2 and a fair exam question.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
The sum of k2 for k running from 1 to 10.
Find
Its value, and the value of the sum of (3k + 2) over the same range.
Formula
∑ k2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6 and ∑ k = n(n + 1) / 2, with the two splitting rules above.

The squares, at n = 10:

10 × 11 × 21 / 6 = 2310 / 6 = 385

The linear one. Split it first, which is where the rules earn their place:

∑ (3k + 2) = 3 ∑ k + ∑ 2
= 3 × (10 × 11 / 2) + 10 × 2
= 3 × 55 + 20
= 165 + 20 = 185

Note the second term. Summing the constant 2 ten times gives 20, not 2. Forgetting that a constant inside a sum still gets added once per index is the standard slip here.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. Define a sequence, and say what a term is.

2. What distinguishes an arithmetic progression from a geometric one? Give one example of each.

3. Write the n-th term of an arithmetic progression and say what every letter means.

4. Write the sum of the first n terms of a geometric progression, and state its condition.

5. Find the rule behind 4, 8, 16, 32 and give its 10th term.

6. Evaluate the sum of the first 5 cubes.

Answers

1. A function from a subset of the integers to a set; a term an is the image of the index n, that is the number in position n.
2. Arithmetic adds a constant difference d, geometric multiplies by a constant ratio r. For example 7, 12, 17, 22 with d = 5, and 4, 8, 16, 32 with r = 2.
3. an = a + (n − 1)d: a is the first term, d the common difference, n the position, and n − 1 the number of steps taken.
4. Sn = a(rn − 1) / (r − 1), valid for r ≠ 1; at r = 1 the sum is na.
5. Geometric, a = 4, r = 2, so an = 4 × 2n−1 = 2n+1, and a10 = 2048.
6. (5 × 6 / 2)2 = 152 = 225.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. In an arithmetic progression the fixed amount added is the common .
  2. In a geometric progression the fixed multiplier is the common .
  3. The n-th term of a geometric progression is .
  4. An infinite geometric series has a finite sum only when r lies between and .
  5. The sum of the first n squares is .
  6. 1, 5, 17, 53, 161, 485 follows the rule an = .
Answers

1. difference. 2. ratio. 3. arn−1. 4. −1, 1. 5. n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6. 6. 3an−1 + 2, with a1 = 1.

blocks.label: Every test question on sequences and progressions
blocks.tag: add for arithmetic, multiply for geometric

title: The Product and Sum Rules
lead:
Two rules answer most counting questions on these papers, and
  choosing between them is the whole skill. Stages multiply. Alternatives add.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, answer the small question at the end of it, then slide the card down: the next frame opens with the answer. Do not read ahead. Being wrong here is the point.

frames.teach: The product rule: if a task has two independent stages with m and n ways, the whole task has m times n ways. The word is AND.
frames.ask: Three shirts and four trousers. How many outfits?

frames.check: 12. Shirt AND trousers, so multiply.
frames.teach: The sum rule: if a task can be done in one way OR another and the ways cannot overlap, add them.
frames.ask: Travel by one of 3 buses or one of 2 trains. How many ways?

frames.check: 5. Bus OR train, so add.
frames.teach: So the whole of counting starts with one word: AND means multiply, OR means add.
frames.ask: Which rule needs the options to be mutually exclusive?

frames.check: the sum rule. If they overlap you must subtract the overlap, which is inclusion-exclusion.
frames.teach: A factorial, n exclamation mark, is the product of every whole number down to 1, and 0 factorial is defined as 1.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will be able to break a counting task into parts, decide whether those parts are compulsory or alternative, apply the product rule, the sum rule and the subtraction rule, and answer the auditorium chairs, ATM PIN, three-digit-number and password questions in full.

blocks.text: What a counting question is asking

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
A counting question asks how many objects of some kind exist. The honest way to answer is to list them all and count the list. That works for six letters and fails for a million PIN codes, so we need rules that give the size of the list without writing it out.

Every such rule comes from the same move: break the task into parts, count each part, then combine. The only question is how to combine, and there are exactly two answers.

If the parts areThenBecause
compulsory: you do part 1 and part 2 and part 3multiplyevery way of doing part 1 pairs with every way of doing part 2
alternative: you do part 1 or part 2 or part 3, never two at onceaddthe possibilities are separate piles and nothing sits in two piles

Those two words, compulsory and alternative, are the ones the 2025/2026 paper uses when it asks you to name the parts of a task. They are worth learning in exactly that language.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
If a task is carried out in a sequence of stages, and

stage 1 can be done in n1 ways,
stage 2 in n2 ways whatever stage 1 did,
… and stage k in nk ways,

then the whole task can be carried out in

n1 × n2 × … × nk ways.

Where k is the number of stages, one for each decision you must make. ni is the number of choices at stage i. × is ordinary multiplication.

Memory hook: and means times. A shirt and a pair of trousers: 3 shirts and 2 trousers give 6 outfits, not 5. Say the task out loud; if the joining word is "and", multiply.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Draw the choices as a tree. Each stage adds a level, and each complete path from the root to a tip is one outcome. Three first choices, each splitting into two, gives 3 × 2 = 6 tips.

The condition that stage 2 has n2 ways whatever stage 1 did is what makes every branch split the same number of times. If the second choice depended on the first, the branches would have different widths and the count would not be a single product.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
If a task can be done in one of k alternative ways, and

alternative 1 can be done in n1 ways, alternative 2 in n2 ways, … alternative k in nk ways,

and no outcome counts under two alternatives at once, then the task can be done in

n1 + n2 + … + nk ways.

Where k is the number of alternatives, one for each separate case. no overlap is a genuine condition, not decoration. If two alternatives can both produce the same outcome, adding counts that outcome twice.

Memory hook: or means plus. Piles you can choose between are added; stages you must pass through are multiplied.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.tag: The word "or" is not proof of a sum
blocks.html:
English "or" is a bad guide on its own. In the password question below, each character is "an uppercase letter or a digit", and that or is counted by adding: 26 + 10 = 36 symbols. But choosing eight characters is eight compulsory stages, so those 36s are multiplied. One sentence, both rules, in that order.

The reliable test is not the word. It is this question: am I describing one decision with several options, or several decisions I must all make? Options add. Decisions multiply.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
To count the objects with some property, when the ones without it are easier to count:

(number with the property) = (total) − (number without it)

Where total is the count with the condition ignored entirely, which is nearly always the easy number. number without it is the count of the cases the condition rules out, and it must be counted over the same total, not over some smaller pool. the two groups must cover everything between them and share nothing, which is what makes one subtraction exact.

This is the counting form of the complement from section 2.2: the objects with the property and the objects without it fill the whole collection between them and share nothing.

Memory hook: "at least one" means "not none". Whenever a question says at least one, count everything, count the cases with none, and subtract. Counting "at least one" directly means splitting into exactly one, exactly two, exactly three and so on, which is longer and easier to get wrong.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
2.  (a) The chairs of an auditorium are to be labeled with an uppercase English letter followed by a
      positive integer not exceeding 100. What is the largest number of chairs that can be labeled
      differently? (6marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
"labeled" is the American spelling; the paper uses it throughout. The mark text is closed up as "(6marks)", which is how this whole paper prints marks. Neither affects the answer. What does affect the answer is "not exceeding 100": that means 100 is allowed, so the integers run 1 to 100 inclusive and there are 100 of them, not 99.

Break it down
Given
A label is an uppercase English letter followed by a positive integer that is at most 100.
Asked
The largest number of chairs that can be labelled differently, which is the number of distinct labels available.
Parts
Two, and both are compulsory: every label has a letter and a number. So this is the product rule.
Marks say
6 marks for one multiplication is generous, so the marks are for the reasoning: name the two stages, count each, justify the counts, then multiply.
Teaches
This section, 5.1.
Trap
Two of them. "Uppercase English letter" is 26, not 52. "Positive integer not exceeding 100" is 100, not 99 and not 101: positive excludes 0, and not exceeding includes 100.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
label = uppercase letter, then a positive integer at most 100.
Find
How many different labels exist.
Rule
Product rule: the two parts are compulsory.

Stage 1: choose the letter. The uppercase English letters are A to Z, so there are 26 choices.

Stage 2: choose the integer. Positive integers not exceeding 100 are 1, 2, 3, …, 100. Counting them, there are 100 choices.

Stage 2 offers the same 100 numbers whichever letter was picked, so the product rule applies directly:

number of labels = 26 × 100 = 2600

Answer: 2600 chairs can be labelled differently.

Say the last sentence in the paper's own terms: since each chair needs its own label, 2600 is the largest number of chairs that can be labelled differently.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: if the label were two uppercase letters followed by a positive integer not exceeding 100, how many? Three compulsory stages now: 26 × 26 × 100 = 67600.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(b)  ATM PIN code in Nigeria can contain the digits 0,1,2,…,9 and digits may be repeated In
      the light of the above, how many 4 to 6 digit pin codes are there? (5 marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
Two sentences have been run together with no full stop: "digits may be repeated In the light of the above". Read the capital "In" as the start of the second sentence. The phrase "4 to 6 digit" means codes of length 4, length 5 or length 6, and those three lengths are the alternatives that make this a sum-rule question sitting on top of a product-rule one.

Break it down
Given
Each position holds one of the ten digits 0 to 9, and repeats are allowed.
Asked
How many codes of length 4, 5 or 6 there are, in total.
Parts
Two levels. Within one length the positions are compulsory parts, so multiply. Across the three lengths the cases are alternative parts, so add.
Marks say
5 marks for three powers and one addition. Show each length separately, then total. A bare final number risks losing the method marks.
Teaches
This section, 5.1.
Trap
Answering only for 6 digits, or multiplying the three lengths together. A code is 4 or 5 or 6 digits long, never two lengths at once, so the three counts are added.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
Digits 0 to 9, so 10 choices per position. Repetition allowed. Lengths 4, 5 and 6.
Find
The total number of such codes.
Rule
Product rule within a length, sum rule across lengths.

Step 1. Count the codes of each length. Because repeats are allowed, every position still has all 10 digits available, no matter what the earlier positions took. So each position is a stage with 10 ways.

LengthProduct ruleCount
4 digits10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10410000
5 digits105100000
6 digits1061000000

Step 2. Combine the three lengths. A code has exactly one length, so no code is counted twice and the sum rule applies:

total = 104 + 105 + 106
= 10000 + 100000 + 1000000
= 1110000

Answer: there are 1110000 PIN codes of 4 to 6 digits. Written with separators for readability, 1 110 000.

Why repetition matters. If digits could not repeat, each position would remove one digit from the pool and the length-4 count would be 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 instead of 104. Section 5.2 counts that case. The words "digits may be repeated" are the paper telling you which of the two applies.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: how many codes of 4 to 6 digits start with a nonzero digit? Each length loses its first-position zero, giving 9 × 10 3 + 9 × 10 4 + 9 × 10 5 = 9000 + 90000 + 900000 = 999000.

blocks.text: Three-digit numbers, and naming the rule

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(c) i. How many three digit natural numbers can be formed using digits 0, 1, · · · , 9? (1 mark)

      
ii.     Identify the number of parts in the task and the type of the parts (compulsory or
      alternative). (4 marks)

      
iii.    Which rule applies here? (1 mark)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
Parts ii and iii say "the task" and "here" without saying which task. They sit directly under (c) i, and (c) i is the nearest task, so answer them about the three-digit numbers. Part (b) immediately above is also a counting task with a different answer, so the safe examination move is to answer for (c) i and then add one line covering (b) as well. That costs a sentence and cannot be marked wrong. Both answers are given below.

Break it down
Given
The ten digits 0 to 9, and a three-digit natural number to build from them.
Asked
(i) How many such numbers. (ii) Identify the number of parts and their type. (iii) Which rule applies. Only the first is a calculation; the other two ask you to describe your own method.
Marks say
1, 4 and 1. The 4 marks are the largest on this part and they are for the description, not the arithmetic. Name each part, say how many ways it has, and say why it is compulsory.
Teaches
This section, 5.1.
Trap
Answering 103 = 1000. A three-digit number cannot begin with 0, because 012 is the two-digit number 12. The hundreds position has 9 choices, not 10.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
Digits 0 to 9, forming a three-digit natural number.
Find
The count, the parts, and the rule.
Rule
Product rule, with one restricted position.

i. How many three-digit natural numbers

A three-digit natural number runs from 100 to 999. Build it position by position:

PositionAllowed digitsWays
hundreds1 to 9, since a leading 0 would make it a shorter number9
tens0 to 910
units0 to 910

count = 9 × 10 × 10 = 900

Answer: 900. Check it another way, which is worth doing on a 1-mark part: the numbers 100 to 999 inclusive number 999 − 100 + 1 = 900. The two methods agree.

ii. The number of parts and their type

Three parts, all compulsory. Set out in full, since 4 marks are on offer:

  1. Part 1, choose the hundreds digit: 9 ways. Compulsory, because every three-digit number has a hundreds digit.
  2. Part 2, choose the tens digit: 10 ways. Compulsory.
  3. Part 3, choose the units digit: 10 ways. Compulsory.

They are compulsory rather than alternative because the number is not finished until all three have been done. You do not pick one of the three parts; you do part 1 and part 2 and part 3.

For part (b) above, the structure is different and worth one line: that task has three alternative parts, one per allowed length (4, 5 and 6 digits), and each of those parts is itself built from compulsory sub-parts, one per digit position.

iii. Which rule applies

The product rule, because the parts of (c) i are compulsory: the counts 9, 10 and 10 are multiplied.

And again for (b): the sum rule across the three lengths, sitting on top of the product rule within each length.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: how many three-digit natural numbers have no repeated digit? Hundreds 9 ways, tens 9 (zero is back in, but the hundreds digit is gone), units 8. So 9 × 9 × 8 = 648.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(b) Each user on a computer system has a password, which is six to eight characters long, where each
      character is an uppercase letter or a digit. Each password must contain at least one digit. How many
      possible passwords are there? (5 marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
This is the hardest counting question in the whole set, and it is worth 5 marks out of 22.5. It combines all three rules of this section: add across the three lengths, multiply across the character positions, and subtract to handle "at least one digit". Nothing about it is printed wrongly. The difficulty is real, not a defect.

Break it down
Given
Password length 6, 7 or 8. Each character is an uppercase letter or a digit. At least one character must be a digit.
Asked
How many possible passwords there are in total.
Parts
Three alternative lengths, so add. Within a length, one compulsory part per character position, so multiply. The "at least one" condition is handled by subtracting.
Marks say
5 marks. Roughly: 1 for the 36 symbols, 1 for seeing that "at least one digit" means total minus letters-only, 2 for the three lengths, 1 for the total. Show every line.
Teaches
This section, 5.1: product, sum and subtraction rules together.
Trap
Trying to count "at least one digit" directly by cases (exactly one digit, exactly two, and so on). It can be done, but it is seven cases per length and almost nobody finishes it correctly under exam pressure. Subtract instead.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
Length 6, 7 or 8; each character from 26 uppercase letters or 10 digits; at least one digit required.
Find
The number of possible passwords.
Rule
Sum over lengths; product over positions; subtraction for "at least one".

Step 1. Count the symbols available per character. A character is an uppercase letter or a digit, and no symbol is both, so the sum rule gives

26 + 10 = 36 symbols.

Step 2. Turn "at least one digit" into a subtraction. Let Pn be the number of valid passwords of length n. Then

Pn = (all strings of length n over the 36 symbols) − (those using no digit at all)
= 36n − 26n

A string with no digit is made only of the 26 letters, which is where 26n comes from. Every string either contains a digit or does not, and never both, so the subtraction is exact.

Step 3. Evaluate each length.

P6 = 366 − 266 = 2176782336 − 308915776 = 1867866560
P7 = 367 − 267 = 78364164096 − 8031810176 = 70332353920
P8 = 368 − 268 = 2821109907456 − 208827064576 = 2612282842880

Step 4. Add the three lengths. A password has exactly one length, so the sum rule applies:

P = P6 + P7 + P8 = 2684483063360

Answer: 2684483063360 possible passwords, or 2 684 483 063 360 written with separators.

If you run out of time, the formula P = (366 − 266) + (367 − 267) + (368 − 268) with the three rules named earns most of the 5 marks on its own. Write the formula first, then evaluate. Never the other way round.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: same question but passwords are exactly six characters and must contain at least one letter. Answer: 36 6 − 10 6 = 2176782336 − 1000000 = 2175782336.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. When do you multiply the counts of the parts, and when do you add them?

2. What condition must alternatives satisfy before the sum rule is valid?

3. How many three-digit natural numbers are there, and why is it not 1000?

4. Turn "at least one vowel" into a subtraction.

5. Labels are one uppercase letter then an integer from 1 to 100. How many?

Answers

1. Multiply when the parts are compulsory, that is, when all of them must be done. Add when they are alternatives and exactly one of them happens.
2. No outcome may count under two alternatives, otherwise it is counted twice.
3. 900. The hundreds digit cannot be 0, so it has 9 choices, not 10: 9 × 10 × 10.
4. (total number of strings) − (number of strings with no vowel).
5. 26 × 100 = 2600.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. Parts that must all be done are , and their counts are .
  2. Parts you choose between are , and their counts are .
  3. The number of PIN codes of 4 to 6 digits, repeats allowed, is .
  4. "At least one" is counted as total minus .
Answers

1. compulsory, multiplied. 2. alternative, added. 3. 1110000. 4. none.

title: Permutations and Combinations
lead:
One question decides which formula you need: does the order of
  the chosen objects change the answer? If it does, you are permuting. If it does
  not, you are combining.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, answer the small question at the end of it, then slide the card down: the next frame opens with the answer. Do not read ahead. Being wrong here is the point.

frames.teach: The whole topic turns on one question: does order matter? If it does, it is a permutation. If not, a combination.
frames.ask: Choosing a president and a secretary from a club. Order or not?

frames.check: order matters, because the two roles differ. So permutation.
frames.teach: Permutation: nPr = n factorial over (n minus r) factorial. Arrangements of r things chosen from n.
frames.ask: How many ways to arrange 3 of 5 books on a shelf?

frames.teach: Combination: nCr = n factorial over r factorial times (n minus r) factorial. Selections where order is irrelevant.
frames.ask: How many ways to choose 3 of 5 books to take home?

frames.check: 5C3 = 10. Six times fewer, because each selection had 3 factorial orderings.
frames.teach: That is the relationship: nPr = nCr times r factorial. The permutation counts every ordering of every selection.
frames.ask: A committee of 3 from 5 people. Which do you use?

frames.check: combination. A committee has no order.
frames.teach: Ask the order question first, every time, and the formula follows.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will be able to compute factorials, use the permutation and combination formulas, count arrangements of a word with repeated letters, handle "at least one" selections, and answer the SCHOOL, the six boys and four girls, and the prayer partners questions in full.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Section F.1 introduced this notation. It is restated here because every formula in this part is built from it, and you should not have to turn back mid-question.

For a positive integer n, n factorial, written n!, is the product of every positive integer from n down to 1:

n! = n × (n − 1) × (n − 2) × … × 2 × 1

and by definition

0! = 1

Where n is a whole number that is not negative. ! is read "factorial", so 5! is read "five factorial". It is not an exclamation mark and never punctuation.

Memory hook: count down and multiply. And 0! = 1 is not a trick: there is exactly one way to arrange nothing, namely do nothing, so the count is 1, not 0.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: The values you should know by sight
blocks.html:
n01234567810
n!1126241207205040403203628800

Factorials grow violently. That is the reason counting questions ask for an expression as often as a number: 20! has nineteen digits and no examiner wants it written out.

The cancelling trick, which you will use constantly. Because n! = n × (n − 1)!, a ratio of factorials collapses:

10! / 7! = (10 × 9 × 8 × 7!) / 7! = 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

Never compute 10! and 7! separately and divide. Cancel first, always.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
A permutation is an arrangement of objects in a definite order. An r-permutation of n distinct objects is an ordered selection of r of them, and the number of these is

P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!

Where n is how many distinct objects are available. r is how many are being chosen and arranged, with 0 ≤ r ≤ n. P(n, r) is also written nPr or nPr, which is the label printed on most calculators.

The special case r = n: arranging all n objects gives P(n, n) = n! / 0! = n!. Every permutation question about "all of them" is just a factorial.

Memory hook: P for position. A permutation cares where each object lands, so AB and BA are two different answers.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
You already have this from the product rule. To fill r ordered positions from n objects with no repeats:

position 1: n ways
position 2: n − 1 ways, since one object is used up
position 3: n − 2 ways
…
position r: n − r + 1 ways

Multiplying gives n × (n − 1) × … × (n − r + 1), which is r factors counting down from n. Writing that as a ratio of factorials:

n × (n − 1) × … × (n − r + 1) = n! / (n − r)!

because dividing by (n − r)! cancels exactly the tail of the product that we stopped short of. So P(n, r) is not a new idea; it is the product rule packaged.

Worked: P(6, 4) = 6! / 2! = 720 / 2 = 360, and by the counting-down form 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360. The two agree, as they must.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
A combination is a selection of objects without regard to order. The number of ways of choosing r objects from n distinct objects is

C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n − r)!)

Where n is how many objects are available. r is how many are chosen, with 0 ≤ r ≤ n. C(n, r) is also written nCr or nCr.

Why the extra r! Each unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! different orders, and P(n, r) counts every one of those orders separately. Dividing by r! collapses them back into one:

C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r!

Memory hook: C for committee. A committee of three is the same committee however you read out the names, so order is thrown away and you divide by r!.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
Ask the question in this exact form: if I swap two of the chosen objects, is that a different answer?

TaskSwap changes it?Use
Arranging letters into a wordyes, TAB is not BATpermutation
Filling the posts of chair and secretaryyes, the two people swap jobspermutation
Picking 4 students for a teamno, the same four peoplecombination
Choosing a subset of a setno, a set has no ordercombination

The wording that gives it away: arrange, order, line up, rank, first and second point to a permutation; select, choose, pick, committee, team, subset, group point to a combination.

One warning about that list. It is a guide, not a law. Read the task, not the verb: a question that says "select" and then gives the chosen people different jobs is a permutation despite the word.

blocks.text: Arranging a word with repeated letters

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
The number of distinct arrangements of n objects, of which one kind repeats n1 times, another n2 times, and so on, is

n! / (n1! × n2! × … × nk!)

Where n is the total number of objects, letters counted as often as they appear. ni is how many times the i-th repeated object occurs. Objects appearing once contribute 1! = 1 and can be left out.

Why divide. Pretend the repeats are distinguishable for a moment, say O1 and O2. Then all n objects are distinct and there are n! arrangements. But swapping O1 and O2 produces a word that looks identical, so every genuine word has been counted 2! times. Divide by 2! to correct it.

Memory hook: divide out what you cannot tell apart. One factorial on the bottom for each repeated letter, using how many times it repeats.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(d) Find out the number of ways that the letters of the word "SCHOOL" can be arranged?
      (2½ marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
A command punctuated as a question, which this paper does in several places. Nothing else is wrong with it, and the quotation marks around the word are the paper's own. The word is the whole difficulty: SCHOOL has six letters and the letter O appears twice.

Break it down
Given
The six letters of the word SCHOOL: S, C, H, O, O, L.
Asked
The number of ways they can be arranged. Arranged means ordered, so this is a permutation.
Marks say
2.5 marks. That is enough for the formula, the substitution and the answer, and not enough to list 360 words. Do not list them.
Teaches
This section, 5.2.
Trap
Answering 6! = 720. The two O's are identical, so half of those 720 orderings spell the same word twice over. The answer is 360.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
The letters S, C, H, O, O, L. Total n = 6, with the letter O repeated twice.
Find
The number of distinct arrangements.
Formula
n! divided by the factorial of each repeat count.

Step 1. Count the letters and the repeats.

LetterSCHOL
Times it occurs11121

Total letters n = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6. One letter repeats, namely O, and it repeats twice.

Step 2. Apply the formula.

arrangements = 6! / 2!
= 720 / 2
= 360

Answer: the letters of SCHOOL can be arranged in 360 ways.

State the reasoning in one line for the marker: if the six letters were all different there would be 6! = 720 arrangements, but swapping the two O's changes nothing visible, so every distinct word has been counted 2! times and 720 must be halved.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: how many arrangements has the word LEVEL? Five letters with L twice and E twice, so 5! / (2! 2!) = 120 / 4 = 30.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(b) In a group of students, there are 6 boys and 4 girls. Out of 10 students, 4 students have to be
      selected. Find out how many different ways the students can be selected such that at least one
      boy should be selected. (5 marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
"Out of 10 students" restates what the first sentence already said, since 6 + 4 = 10. That is a helpful redundancy rather than a defect: it confirms the ten students are the whole pool. The phrase to act on is "at least one boy", which is the subtraction rule of section 5.1 in a combination setting.

Break it down
Given
6 boys and 4 girls, 10 students in all. Four are to be selected.
Asked
How many different ways the selection can be made with at least one boy among the four.
Order
A group of four is selected, with no jobs or ranking attached, so order does not matter. This is a combination.
Marks say
5 marks. Enough for the total, the excluded case, the subtraction and a check. Showing the case-by-case method as a verification is worth doing if time allows.
Teaches
This section, 5.2, using the subtraction rule from 5.1.
Trap
Reading "at least one boy" as "exactly one boy" and answering C(6, 1) × C(4, 3) = 24. At least one means one, two, three or four.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
6 boys, 4 girls, 10 students; choose 4.
Find
The number of selections containing at least one boy.
Formula
C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n − r)!), with the subtraction rule for "at least one".

Step 1. Count all selections of four, ignoring the condition.

C(10, 4) = 10! / (4! × 6!)
= (10 × 9 × 8 × 7) / (4 × 3 × 2 × 1)
= 5040 / 24
= 210

Step 2. Count the selections that break the condition. A selection fails only when it contains no boy, that is, when all four chosen are girls. There are exactly 4 girls, so all four must be taken:

C(4, 4) = 4! / (4! × 0!) = 1

Note 0! = 1 here; that definition is doing real work.

Step 3. Subtract.

at least one boy = 210 − 1 = 209

Answer: 209 different selections contain at least one boy.

Verification by cases, which is the long way and a good check:

BoysGirlsWaysValue
13C(6, 1) × C(4, 3)6 × 4 = 24
22C(6, 2) × C(4, 2)15 × 6 = 90
31C(6, 3) × C(4, 1)20 × 4 = 80
40C(6, 4) × C(4, 0)15 × 1 = 15

24 + 90 + 80 + 15 = 209. The two methods agree.

The case table also shows why subtracting is the better exam move: four combinations and three additions, against one subtraction.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: how many selections of four contain at least one girl? Total 210, minus the all-boy selections C(6, 4) = 15, gives 195.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(c) Suppose 10 male and 10 female students needs to pray with one another in a one male-one female
      order:

      
(i)     How many Prayer sessions will there be? (1 mark)

      
(ii)    How many prayer units are generated here? (1½ marks)

      
(iii)   Calculate the choice of prayer partners. (3 marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
Two things to flag. First, "students needs" does not agree in number, and "Prayer" is capitalised in (i) but not in (ii). Those are harmless. Second, and this one matters: the paper never says what a session is or what a unit is, so parts (i) and (ii) can be read more than one way. The answer below states the reading it uses before computing anything, gives the numbers that reading produces, and then gives the other reading's numbers too. Part (iii) is unambiguous and carries the most marks.

Break it down
Given
10 male and 10 female students. They pray in pairs, each pair being one male and one female.
Asked
(i) the number of sessions, (ii) the number of units, (iii) calculate the choice of prayer partners.
Marks say
1, 1.5 and 3. The weight is on (iii), which is a full permutation, so budget your time there. Parts (i) and (ii) are one line each.
Teaches
This section, 5.2, with the product rule from 5.1.
Trap
Answering (iii) with 10 × 10 = 100. That counts the possible pairs, which is part (ii). The choice of partners means assigning every male a different female at once, and that is 10!.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
10 males, 10 females, praying one male with one female.
Find
Sessions, units, and the number of ways to choose partners.
Rule
Product rule for the pairs, permutation for the assignment.

Step 0. State the reading. Write this on the script before answering, because the paper does not supply it:

A prayer unit is one male paired with one female. A session is one round in which all twenty students are paired at the same time, giving ten units per session. Every male is to pray with every female.

i. How many prayer sessions

In one session each of the 10 males prays with one female, so a session uses up 10 of the possible male-female pairings. Every male must eventually meet all 10 females, so each male needs 10 turns:

number of sessions = 10

ii. How many prayer units

A unit is one male with one female. Choosing the male is 10 ways and choosing the female is 10 ways, and both choices must be made, so the product rule gives

units = 10 × 10 = 100

Consistency check: 10 sessions with 10 units in each is 100 units, which matches. The two answers agree, which is exactly why stating the reading first was worth a line.

iii. Calculate the choice of prayer partners

Now the real work. In a single session, every male is given a different female. Line the males up in a fixed order and hand out the females:

male 1: 10 choices of partner
male 2: 9 choices, since one female is taken
male 3: 8 choices
…
male 10: 1 choice

All ten choices must be made, so the product rule applies:

choices = 10 × 9 × 8 × … × 2 × 1 = 10! = 3628800

In the language of this section, the ten females are being arranged among the ten males, so the count is P(10, 10) = 10! / 0! = 10!.

Answer: 3628800 ways, or 3 628 800 with separators.

The other reading, for safety. If instead a "session" means a single male-female meeting, then there are 100 sessions and 10 units in each round. Whichever reading a marker has in mind, the two numbers on the table are 10 and 100, and part (iii) is 10! = 3628800 either way. Writing your reading down protects the marks.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: with 5 males and 5 females, the units are 5 × 5 = 25 and the choice of partners is 5! = 120.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. State the formulas for P(n, r) and C(n, r).

2. What is 0!, and why?

3. Which is larger, P(8, 3) or C(8, 3), and by what factor?

4. How many arrangements has the word SCHOOL, and why is it not 720?

5. Four students are picked from ten for a team. Permutation or combination?

Answers

1. P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)! and C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n − r)!).
2. 0! = 1, because there is exactly one way to arrange nothing.
3. P(8, 3) is larger, by a factor of 3! = 6: P(8, 3) = 336 and C(8, 3) = 56.
4. 360. The two O's are identical, so 6! counts every word twice and must be divided by 2!.
5. A combination: the team is the same team however the names are ordered.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. An arrangement in a definite order is a .
  2. A selection with no regard to order is a .
  3. C(n, r) is P(n, r) divided by .
  4. Choosing 4 from 10 can be done in ways.
  5. Ten males paired with ten females can be partnered in ways.
Answers

1. permutation. 2. combination. 3. r!. 4. 210. 5. 3628800.

title: Inclusion, Exclusion and the Pigeonhole Principle
lead:
When two groups overlap, adding their sizes counts the overlap
  twice. Subtracting it once is the whole of inclusion and exclusion, and it is
  worth seven marks on the newest paper.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, answer the small question at the end of it, then slide the card down: the next frame opens with the answer. Do not read ahead. Being wrong here is the point.

frames.teach: Counting a union by adding the two sets double counts the overlap, so you subtract it once: the size of A union B is size A plus size B minus size of the intersection.
frames.ask: 30 study maths, 25 study physics, 10 study both. How many study at least one?

frames.check: 45. That is 30 plus 25 minus 10.
frames.teach: For THREE sets the pattern alternates: add the three singles, subtract the three pairs, add the triple back.
frames.ask: Why is the triple overlap added back at the end?

frames.check: because subtracting the three pairs removed it three times after it was added three times, leaving it at zero.
frames.teach: The pigeonhole principle is the other half of this module: if there are more objects than boxes, at least one box holds more than one object.
frames.ask: Thirteen people in a room. Why must two share a birth month?

frames.check: thirteen objects, twelve boxes.
frames.teach: The general form: n objects into m boxes forces some box to hold at least the ceiling of n over m.

blocks.html: By the end of this section you will be able to state and apply the inclusion and exclusion principle for two and three sets, read the overlap off a Venn diagram, state the pigeonhole principle in both its forms, and answer the Ibibio and Efik question and the class-size question in full.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
The sum rule of section 5.1 came with a condition: no outcome may count under two alternatives. Sets of people almost always break that condition, because a person can be in both.

Suppose 30 students take Maths and 25 take Physics. Adding gives 55. But if 10 take both, those 10 were counted once in the 30 and again in the 25, so 55 overstates the class by exactly 10. The true total is 45.

That is the entire idea. Add the parts, then take the overlap back out once, because it went in twice.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Section 2.2 introduced this as the counting formula, where it belonged with the set operations. Here it is again, this time with the rearrangements the exam actually asks for.

For any two finite sets A and B,

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

Where n(A) is the cardinality of A, the number of things in it, as defined in section 2.1. A ∪ B is the union: everything in A or in B or in both. A ∩ B is the intersection: the things in both, which is the overlap that was counted twice.

The rearrangements you will actually use. Exam questions give you three of the four quantities and ask for the fourth, so learn all three forms, not just the first:

n(A ∩ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∪ B)     [find the overlap]
n(A only) = n(A) − n(A ∩ B)     [strip the overlap out of A]
n(B only) = n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

Memory hook: in, in, out. Put A in, put B in, take the middle out. And a completed answer always satisfies A only + both + B only = n(A ∪ B).

The principle of inclusion and exclusion

The claim. The size of a union is found by adding the sizes of the sets and then removing every overlap that the addition counted more than once. For two sets that means subtracting the single overlap; for more sets the corrections alternate in sign.

In symbols.
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)

Conditions. The sets must be finite, or the counts do not exist to be added. Nothing else is required: the sets may overlap in any way at all, which is precisely the point of the principle.

The limiting case. When the sets are disjoint, every overlap term is 0 and the principle collapses to the sum rule of section 5.1: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B). So the sum rule is not a separate law but the special case of this one where nothing is shared.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
For three finite sets A, B and C,

n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)

Where n(A), n(B), n(C) are the sizes of the three sets on their own, each counted with no regard to the others. n(A ∩ B) and the other two pair terms are the sizes of each two-way overlap, subtracted because each was counted in two of the singles. n(A ∩ B ∩ C) is the size of the three-way overlap, added back because the singles put it in three times and the pairs took it out three times.

Read the pattern rather than memorising the letters: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add the triple. Signs alternate, and the number of sets in each term goes up by one.

The final term is added back because the elements in all three sets were added three times by the singles and then subtracted three times by the pairs, leaving them counted zero times. One addition restores them.

Memory hook: plus singles, minus pairs, plus triple. Odd-sized groups are added, even-sized groups are subtracted.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(a) In a group of 100 students, 72 students can speak Ibibio and 43 students can speak Ibibio.
      Based on these data, answer the following questions:

      
(i)     Find the number of students who can speak both Ibibio and Efik. (3 marks)

      
(ii)    Find the number of students who can speak Ibibio only. (2 marks)

      
(iii)   Find the number of students who can speak Efik only. (2 marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
This question contradicts itself, and it is the most important defect on the paper. The opening sentence names the same language twice: "72 students can speak Ibibio and 43 students can speak Ibibio". Parts (i) to (iii) then ask about Ibibio and Efik, so the second figure must have been meant as Efik. Read literally, the data mention Efik nowhere and 7 marks are unanswerable.

What to do in the hall. Do not stall and do not silently rewrite the question. Write one line: "The second figure is taken as 43 students who can speak Efik, since parts (i) to (iii) ask about Efik and the question is otherwise unanswerable." Then answer on that reading. A stated assumption that is obviously the intended one is normal mathematical practice and protects every mark; a silent one does not.

Break it down
Given
100 students in the group. 72 speak Ibibio. 43 speak Efik, on the stated reading.
Asked
(i) both languages, (ii) Ibibio only, (iii) Efik only. Three different regions of the same diagram.
Hidden assumption
That every one of the 100 speaks at least one of the two, so n(A ∪ B) = 100. The question does not say so, but without it the three parts have no unique answer. State this too.
Marks say
3, 2 and 2. Part (i) is worth more because the other two follow from it in one subtraction each. Get (i) right and the rest are free.
Teaches
This section, 5.3.
Trap
Answering (ii) with 72. That is everyone who speaks Ibibio, including those who also speak Efik. "Only" means the overlap must come out.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
n(U) = 100, n(I) = 72 speak Ibibio, n(E) = 43 speak Efik.
Find
n(I ∩ E), then n(I only) and n(E only).
Formula
n(I ∪ E) = n(I) + n(E) − n(I ∩ E).

Step 0. State the two readings you are working under.

  1. The second figure of 43 refers to Efik, not Ibibio.
  2. Every student speaks at least one of the two languages, so n(I ∪ E) = 100.

Assumption 2 is forced by the arithmetic as well as by common sense: 72 + 43 = 115, which is 15 more than the group, so at least 15 students must be in both. If some students spoke neither, the overlap would be even larger, and the question gives no way to know how many.

i. Students who speak both

Rearrange the two-set formula to make the overlap the subject:

n(I ∩ E) = n(I) + n(E) − n(I ∪ E)
= 72 + 43 − 100
= 115 − 100
= 15

Answer: 15 students speak both Ibibio and Efik.

ii. Students who speak Ibibio only

The 72 Ibibio speakers include the 15 who also speak Efik. Strip them out:

n(I only) = n(I) − n(I ∩ E) = 72 − 15 = 57

iii. Students who speak Efik only

n(E only) = n(E) − n(I ∩ E) = 43 − 15 = 28

Check, and write the check down. The three regions must fill the group exactly:

57 + 15 + 28 = 100   ✓

Drawing this diagram is worth doing even when the question does not ask for it. It takes twenty seconds and it catches the "only" trap automatically.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: in a group of 80, 50 speak Yoruba and 45 speak Hausa, everyone speaking at least one. Both: 50 + 45 − 80 = 15. Yoruba only: 35. Hausa only: 30. Check: 35 + 15 + 30 = 80.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(b) In a discrete structures' class, every student is a major in either Computer Science or Maths
      or both. There of 25 students who major in Computer, while 13 in Maths. If 8 students major
      in both Computing Science & Maths, how many students are in the entire class? (4marks)

blocks.html:
Note on the paper
"There of 25 students" is a typing slip for "There are 25 students", and the subject is called "Computer Science" in one clause, "Computer" in the next and "Computing Science" in the third. All three name the same set. The sentence that saves the question is the first one: every student majors in Computer Science or Maths or both, which states outright the assumption that the Ibibio question left you to supply. So here n(A ∪ B) is the class, and it is what you are asked for.

Break it down
Given
n(C) = 25 major in Computer Science, n(M) = 13 major in Maths, n(C ∩ M) = 8 major in both, and nobody majors in neither.
Asked
How many students are in the entire class, which is n(C ∪ M).
Marks say
4 marks for one formula. Write the principle, then substitute, then evaluate, then answer in a sentence. A bare 30 earns less.
Teaches
This section, 5.3.
Trap
Answering 25 + 13 = 38, forgetting the 8 who were counted in both figures.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
Given
n(C) = 25, n(M) = 13, n(C ∩ M) = 8, every student in at least one.
Find
n(C ∪ M), the size of the class.
Formula
n(C ∪ M) = n(C) + n(M) − n(C ∩ M).

Because every student majors in one subject or the other or both, the class is the union, so the union is what to compute:

n(C ∪ M) = 25 + 13 − 8
= 38 − 8
= 30

Answer: there are 30 students in the entire class.

Break it into regions as a check: Computer Science only is 25 − 8 = 17, Maths only is 13 − 8 = 5, and both is 8. Then 17 + 5 + 8 = 30, which agrees.

One ambiguity worth a line on the script. The sentence "There of 25 students who major in Computer" could be misread as saying the class has 25 students in total. It cannot mean that: 8 of them major in both, and 13 major in Maths, so Maths-only alone would need 5 more students than a 25-strong class has room for once the 25 Computer Science majors are placed. The reading above is the only consistent one.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: if instead 30 major in Computer Science, 20 in Maths and 12 in both, the class has 30 + 20 − 12 = 38 students.

blocks.html:
The pigeonhole principle

The claim. If more objects are placed into boxes than there are boxes, then some box must hold more than one object. Nothing about the objects, the boxes or the way they are placed can prevent it.

In symbols.
If k + 1 or more objects go into k boxes, some box holds at least 2.
If N objects go into k boxes, some box holds at least ⌈N / k⌉.

Conditions. The number of boxes must be finite, and every object must go into some box. It says nothing about which box is crowded, and it cannot: that is a feature, since it lets you prove something exists without being able to find it.

The limiting case. When N = k the principle promises only ⌈k / k⌉ = 1, which is no information at all, and correctly so: k objects can sit one to a box with nothing shared. The principle bites from N = k + 1 onward, and that single extra object is the whole of it.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
If k + 1 or more objects are placed into k boxes, then at least one box contains two or more objects.

Where k is the number of boxes, sometimes called pigeonholes. objects are whatever is being sorted into them: people, numbers, letters, socks.

The generalised form, which is the one that answers real questions: if N objects are placed into k boxes, then at least one box contains at least

⌈N / k⌉ objects,

where ⌈x⌉ is the ceiling of x: the smallest whole number that is not less than x. So ⌈7 / 3⌉ = ⌈2.33 ⌉ = 3.

Memory hook: more pigeons than holes means sharing. The principle never tells you which box is crowded, only that one of them is. That is exactly why it is useful: it proves something exists without finding it.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Every pigeonhole argument has the same three steps, and the marks are in step 2.

  1. Name the objects. What is being placed?
  2. Name the boxes. This is the creative step. The boxes are usually the possible values of something, not physical containers.
  3. Compare the counts and apply the principle.

Example. Among any 13 people, at least two were born in the same month. Objects: the 13 people. Boxes: the 12 months. Since 13 > 12, two people share a box, that is, a birth month.

Example, generalised form. Among 100 people, at least ⌈100 / 12⌉ = ⌈8.33⌉ = 9 share a birth month.

Example with an unobvious box. In any group of 8 people, two have the same number of friends within the group. Objects: 8 people. Boxes: the possible friend counts, 0 to 7, which is 8 boxes, so the counting alone is not enough. The extra step: nobody can have 0 friends and somebody else have 7 at the same time, because a person with 7 friends is friends with everyone, including the supposed loner. So only 7 of the 8 boxes can be occupied, and 8 people into 7 boxes forces a repeat.

Where this stands on the papers: none of the five papers we hold has set a pigeonhole question outright. It is in the official course text, it takes two minutes to learn, and the 2023/2024 paper does ask a closely related impossibility question about five cities that is settled by a counting argument in Part Six. Learn the statement and the three steps; that is the whole of the return on it.

blocks.label: Recall and check
blocks.question:
1. State the inclusion and exclusion principle for two sets.

2. 40 students take Maths, 30 take Physics, 12 take both and everyone takes at least one. How many students are there?

3. In the same group, how many take Maths only?

4. Write the three-set formula from the pattern, without looking.

5. State the pigeonhole principle, and say what ⌈17 / 5⌉ is.

Answers

1. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
2. 40 + 30 − 12 = 58.
3. 40 − 12 = 28.
4. Add the three singles, subtract the three pairs, add the triple.
5. If k + 1 or more objects go into k boxes, some box holds two or more. ⌈17 / 5⌉ = ⌈3.4⌉ = 4.

blocks.label: Fill in the gap
blocks.html:
1. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − .
  2. The number who speak Ibibio only is 72 minus , giving .
  3. In the three-set formula the pairs are and the triple is .
  4. Placing 10 objects into 3 boxes forces some box to hold at least .
Answers

1. n(A ∩ B). 2. 15, 57. 3. subtracted, added. 4. ⌈10 / 3⌉ = 4.
