blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
a. Five differences, with two examples each (10 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 6.1. Each pair needs a contrasting sentence, not two definitions: see F.2.

i. Degree versus valency of a node. They are two names for the same quantity, the number of edge ends meeting at a vertex, whereas "valency" is the older term borrowed from chemistry and "degree" is the one this syllabus uses elsewhere. Examples: in a triangle every vertex has degree 2 and equally valency 2; a pendant vertex has degree 1 and valency 1.

ii. Predicate versus propositional logic. A proposition is either true or false outright, whereas a predicate has a variable in it and only becomes true or false once the variable is given a value. Examples: "3 is prime" is a proposition; "x is prime" is a predicate P(x), true at x = 3 and false at x = 4.

iii. Universal versus existential quantifier. ∀x claims the predicate holds for every value in the domain, whereas ∃x claims it holds for at least one. Examples: over the integers ∀x(x2 ≥ 0) is true; ∃x(x2 = 4) is true, and ∀x(x2 = 4) is false.

iv. Adjacency versus path matrix. The adjacency matrix records whether two vertices are joined by a single edge, whereas the path matrix records whether one can be reached from the other by any sequence of edges. Examples: in the path a to b to c, the adjacency matrix has 0 in the (a, c) position but the path matrix has 1; in a complete graph the two matrices agree everywhere off the diagonal.

v. Logical matrix versus relation matrix. A logical matrix is any matrix whose entries are the truth values 0 and 1, whereas a relation matrix is a logical matrix used specifically to record a relation, with mij = 1 exactly when (i, j) is in the relation. Examples: an adjacency matrix is a logical matrix; the matrix of "divides" on {1, 2, 3, 4} is a relation matrix.

b. i. Nine types of set (3 marks) ii. Two ways to describe a set (2 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 2.1.

i. Empty {}, singleton {5}, finite {1, 2, 3}, infinite ℕ, equal ({1,2} and {2,1}), equivalent ({1,2} and {a,b}), subset ({1} of {1,2}), universal (U, everything under discussion), and power set (all subsets of a set).

ii. Roster form, listing the members between braces, and set-builder form, stating the property they share: {x | x is a positive prime below 10}.

c. A = {11, 12, 13, 14}, B = {13, 14, 15, 16} (2.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 2.2.

A ∩ B = {13, 14}
A − B = {11, 12}
B − A = {15, 16}

Each is checked by reading A once and asking of each member whether it is in B.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
a. Five justifications for the subject (5 marks)

Quoted as printed in Foundations F.1. One mark each, so five distinct points with an application named in each.

1. It is the mathematics of the computer itself, which stores and processes separated values rather than a continuum. 2. Logic is the basis of circuit design and of program correctness, as Part Eight shows for gates and Part One for conditions. 3. Graphs and trees are the standard data models for networks, file systems, compilers and routing. 4. Counting gives complexity and capacity analysis: how many passwords, how many states, how many operations. 5. Proof and induction justify algorithms, which is how one shows a program is right for every input rather than for the ones tested.

b. S × C where S has 3 and C has 2 members (2 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 2.3. The Cartesian product is every ordered pair with the first from S and the second from C, so there are 3 × 2 = 6 of them:

{(John, CSC701), (John, CSC702), (Mary, CSC701), (Mary, CSC702), (Peter, CSC701), (Peter, CSC702)}

c. Is R reflexive? (2 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 3.3. R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4), (1,2), (2,3)} on {1, 2, 3, 4}.

Yes. Reflexivity requires (a, a) for every a in the set. All four loops (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4) are present, so R is reflexive. The extra pairs (1,2) and (2,3) do not affect reflexivity.

d. Is R an equivalence relation? (4 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 3.3. Three properties, each checked explicitly, which is what "detailed explanation" is asking for.

Reflexive: (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4) are all present. Yes.
Symmetric: the non-loop pairs are (1,3) and (3,1), (2,4) and (4,2). Each appears with its reverse. Yes.
Transitive: (1,3) with (3,1) needs (1,1), present; (3,1) with (1,3) needs (3,3), present; (2,4) with (4,2) needs (2,2), present; (4,2) with (2,4) needs (4,4), present. No other composable pair exists. Yes.

So R is an equivalence relation, and it partitions {1, 2, 3, 4} into the classes {1, 3} and {2, 4}. Naming the classes is the line that shows you know what an equivalence relation is for.

e. Partially versus totally ordered, and the CGPA table (4.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 3.4.

The difference. In a partially ordered set some pairs may be incomparable, whereas in a totally ordered set every two elements are comparable. Both orders are reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; total order adds comparability.

The table. A has 4.80, B has 4.50, C has 4.10. Order them by "has a CGPA at least as high as". Every pair can be compared, because any two real numbers can: 4.80 ≥ 4.50 ≥ 4.10.

Proof that it is a total order. Reflexive, since each student's CGPA is at least as high as itself. Antisymmetric, since if two are each at least as high as the other their CGPAs are equal and, these three being distinct, the students are the same. Transitive, by the transitivity of ≥ on the reals. Comparable, since ≥ compares any two reals. Therefore totally ordered, and the chain is A, then B, then C.

blocks.working:
a. 100 students, two languages (7 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 5.3.

State the reading first. The question as printed names Ibibio twice, for both the 72 and the 43, which would make the two figures describe one group and leave nothing to compute. The only reading that makes the question answerable, and the one taken here, is that 72 speak Ibibio and 43 speak Efik. Say that in one line before computing anything.

(i) Both. Every student speaks at least one, so the union is 100:

n(I ∪ E) = n(I) + n(E) − n(I ∩ E)
100 = 72 + 43 − n(I ∩ E)
n(I ∩ E) = 115 − 100 = 15

(ii) Ibibio only. 72 − 15 = 57

(iii) Efik only. 43 − 15 = 28

Check: 57 + 15 + 28 = 100. The three regions of the diagram account for every student, which is the one-line verification worth writing.

b. Four from six boys and four girls, at least one boy (5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 5.2. "At least one" means total minus none.

total committees = C(10, 4) = 210
with no boy, that is all four girls = C(4, 4) = 1
at least one boy = 210 − 1 = 209

Why not add up the cases. C(6,1)C(4,3) + C(6,2)C(4,2) + C(6,3)C(4,1) + C(6,4) = 24 + 90 + 80 + 15 = 209 as well, but it is four computations where the complement is one.

c. Ten male and ten female praying in pairs (5.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 5.2.

(i) Sessions. Each session pairs one male with one female and every person prays once per round, so ten pairs form at a time and there are 10 sessions if each male is to pray with each female.

(ii) Prayer units. Every male paired with every female is 10 × 10 = 100 distinct units, by the product rule.

(iii) Choice of prayer partners. Fix the order of the males and assign the females to them; that is an arrangement of ten distinct people in ten positions:

10! = 3628800

Say which reading you used. The three parts are answered here as "one round of ten pairs at a time, ten rounds in all", and stating that protects every mark below it.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
a. Short notes with examples, five items (10 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 6.1. Two marks each, so each item wants a definition and an example.

i. Size of a graph. The number of edges, written |E|. In the complete graph K4 the size is 6; in a tree on 10 vertices the size is 9.

ii. Valency of a vertex. The number of edge ends meeting at it, the same quantity as its degree. A pendant vertex has valency 1; every vertex of K5 has valency 4.

iii. In-degree and out-degree. In a directed graph the in-degree of v is how many arrows arrive at v and the out-degree how many leave. If a to b and c to b are the only arcs, then b has in-degree 2 and out-degree 0, while a has out-degree 1 and in-degree 0.

iv. Graph isomorphism. Two graphs are isomorphic when there is a one-to-one correspondence between their vertices that preserves adjacency: the same graph drawn twice. A square drawn as a square and the same four vertices drawn as a diamond are isomorphic; K3 and a path on three vertices are not, since they have different numbers of edges.

v. Eulerian graph. A graph containing a circuit that uses every edge exactly once and returns to its start, which happens exactly when the graph is connected and every vertex has even degree. A triangle is Eulerian; the Konigsberg graph, with four odd-degree vertices, is not.

b. The place of logic in computer science (2 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 1.5. Logic supplies the rules that separate a valid argument from an invalid one, and computing rests on it at every level: circuit design builds directly from AND, OR and NOT (Part Eight); program conditions and loop tests are propositions; database queries are predicate logic; and proving a program correct is proving an implication.

c. Three acceptable logic statements leading to a conclusion (3 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 1.5. A valid argument, laid out as premises and conclusion:

If a program compiles, it has no syntax error.
If it has no syntax error, the parser accepted it.
This program compiles.
∴ The parser accepted it.

Naming the rules earns the marks: the first two premises chain by hypothetical syllogism to give "if it compiles, the parser accepted it", and with the third premise modus ponens gives the conclusion.

d. Arrangements of the letters of SCHOOL (2.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 5.2. Six letters with O repeated twice:

6! / 2! = 720 / 2 = 360

Why the division. The two O's are identical, so each distinct arrangement has been counted 2! = 2 times by 6!, once for each way of ordering them.

blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
a. i. The laboratory door (4.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 8.1. Let A = 1 when a valid card is presented, B = 1 when the fingerprint is correct, D = 1 when the door opens. The door opens only when both are presented, so

D = A · B

which is 1 in exactly one of the four cases.

ABD = A · BDoor
000shut
010shut
100shut
111opens

a. ii. The alarm (3 marks)

Let F and S be the two sensors and L the alarm. "Either or" here is the inclusive or, since the alarm must certainly sound if both fire:

L = F + S

With only the smoke sensor active, F = 0 and S = 1, so L = 0 + 1 = 1: the alarm sounds. Had exclusive or been used the alarm would fall silent when both sensors detected danger, which is the sentence that secures the mark.

b. i. Kuratowski's theorem (2 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 6.7. A graph is planar if and only if it contains no subgraph that is a subdivision of K5 or of K3,3. In words: those two graphs are the only obstructions to planarity, and any non-planar graph has a copy of one of them hidden inside it.

b. ii. Why K5 and K3,3 matter (2 marks)

Because by Kuratowski's theorem they are the minimal non-planar graphs: every non-planar graph contains a subdivision of one of them, so the whole question of planarity reduces to looking for these two. They are the reference points against which any drawing is tested.

b. iii. Showing both are non-planar (6 marks)

K5. It has v = 5 vertices and, being complete, e = C(5, 2) = 10 edges. For a simple connected planar graph with v ≥ 3, Euler's formula forces

e ≤ 3v − 6 = 3 × 5 − 6 = 9

but 10 > 9, so the bound fails and K5 is not planar.

K3,3. It has v = 6 and e = 3 × 3 = 9. It is bipartite, so it has no triangle, and the triangle-free bound applies:

e ≤ 2v − 4 = 2 × 6 − 4 = 8

but 9 > 8, so K3,3 is not planar.

Say why the second bound is different. Using e ≤ 3v − 6 on K3,3 gives 12, which 9 satisfies, and the argument would prove nothing. The tighter bound is available precisely because a bipartite graph has no odd cycle and therefore no triangle. That sentence is worth a mark on its own.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
blocks.working:
a. i. The adjacency matrix, explained (2.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 6.5. For a graph on n vertices labelled 1 to n, the adjacency matrix is the n by n array whose entry aij is 1 when vertices i and j are joined by an edge and 0 when they are not. For an undirected graph it is symmetric about the main diagonal, since an edge joining i to j equally joins j to i, and the diagonal is 0 unless the graph has loops.

a. ii. Memory management in an adjacency matrix (4 marks)

The cost. The matrix always occupies n2 entries, whatever the number of edges, because every pair has a slot whether or not it is used.

When that is wasteful. A sparse graph, where the edges are far fewer than n2, stores overwhelmingly zeros. A road network with a thousand junctions and three thousand roads still needs a million entries.

Two ways it is managed. Store only half of it, since symmetry makes the upper triangle sufficient for an undirected graph, roughly halving the space. Or store one bit per entry rather than one integer, since every entry is 0 or 1.

The alternative. An adjacency list keeps, for each vertex, only the vertices actually adjacent to it, so it uses space in proportion to the edges rather than to n2. The trade is speed: the matrix answers "are i and j adjacent" in one lookup, the list has to search.

b. ATM PIN codes of 4 to 6 digits (5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 5.1. Ten digits, repeats allowed, so a code of length k can be formed in 10k ways. The three lengths are alternatives, so add them:

104 + 105 + 106 = 10000 + 100000 + 1000000 = 1110000

Both rules appear here. The product rule gives each 10k, one factor of 10 per position; the sum rule joins the three lengths, because a code has exactly one length.

c. i. Three-digit natural numbers (1 mark)

Quoted as printed in section 5.1. The first digit cannot be 0, so it has 9 choices; the other two have 10 each:

9 × 10 × 10 = 900

Check: the three-digit numbers run from 100 to 999, and 999 − 100 + 1 = 900.

c. ii. The parts of the task, and their type (4 marks)

The task of forming a three-digit number has three parts, choosing the hundreds digit, the tens digit and the units digit. They are compulsory and not alternative: every one must be performed to produce a number, which is exactly the condition the product rule requires. Had they been alternatives, only one would be carried out and the sum rule would apply, as it does across the three PIN lengths in part (b) above.

c. iii. Which rule applies (1 mark)

The product rule, since the three digit choices are performed one after another and every combination of them gives a different number.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.problem: a. Converse, contrapositive and inverse of three conditionals (4.5 marks)
blocks.working:
Quoted as printed in section 1.2. Identify p and q first; that is where the marks are lost, not in the three rewrites.

i. "If it snows tonight, then I will stay at home." p = it snows tonight, q = I will stay at home.

Converse: If I stay at home tonight, then it will snow.
Contrapositive: If I do not stay at home, then it will not snow.
Inverse: If it does not snow tonight, then I will not stay at home.

ii. "I go to the beach whenever it is a sunny summer day." The whenever clause is the hypothesis, so p = it is a sunny summer day, q = I go to the beach. Writing it the other way round loses every mark that follows.

Converse: If I go to the beach, then it is a sunny summer day.
Contrapositive: If I do not go to the beach, then it is not a sunny summer day.
Inverse: If it is not a sunny summer day, then I do not go to the beach.

iii. "When I stay up late, it is necessary that I sleep until noon." "It is necessary that q" makes q the conclusion, so p = I stay up late, q = I sleep until noon.

Converse: If I sleep until noon, then I stayed up late.
Contrapositive: If I do not sleep until noon, then I did not stay up late.
Inverse: If I do not stay up late, then I do not sleep until noon.

b. Four truth tables (4 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 1.1.

i. p ↔ ¬p

p¬pp ↔ ¬p
TFF
FTF

False in every row: it is a contradiction, which is worth saying rather than leaving the marker to notice.

ii. (q → ¬p) ↔ (p ↔ q)

pq¬pq → ¬pp ↔ qthe whole
TTFFTF
TFFTFF
FTTTFF
FFTTTT

True in one row only, when both are false.

iii. (p ⊕ q) ∨ (p ⊕ ¬q)

pqp ⊕ qp ⊕ ¬qthe whole
TTFTT
TFTFT
FTTFT
FFFTT

True in every row: a tautology. The reason is worth one line: p ⊕ q and p ⊕ ¬q are negations of each other, so exactly one of them is true in any row and their disjunction cannot fail.

iv. ((p → q) → r) → s

Four letters, so the table has 24 = 16 rows. Rather than fill sixteen rows blindly, work out where it is false and say so.

Write X for (p → q) → r. The whole expression X → s is false only when X is true and s is false. X is true unless p → q is true and r is false; so X is true when r is true (four ways to choose p and q), or when r is false and p → q is false, which is p true and q false. That is five combinations of p, q, r.

So the expression is false in exactly 5 of the 16 rows, namely those with s false and (p, q, r) equal to (T,T,T), (T,F,T), (F,T,T), (F,F,T) or (T,F,F), and true in the other 11. Draw the full table if time allows; state this if it does not.

c. i. "The home team wins whenever it is raining" (3 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 1.2. With p = "It is raining" and q = "The home team wins", the statement is p → q.

Contrapositive: If the home team does not win, then it is not raining.
Converse: If the home team wins, then it is raining.
Inverse: If it is not raining, then the home team does not win.

c. ii. Prove only the contrapositive agrees (6 marks)

To prove: of the converse, the inverse and the contrapositive, only the contrapositive has the same truth value as p → q in every case.

Proof, by exhaustive truth table. There are only four assignments, so this covers every case and is a complete proof, not an illustration.

pqp → q¬q → ¬pq → p¬p → ¬q
TTTTTT
TFFFTT
FTTTFF
FFTTTT

Read the columns. The contrapositive column is identical to the original in all four rows, so p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p. The converse and the inverse each differ from the original in two rows, the second and the third, so neither is equivalent to it. □

Using the statement from c(i), as the question asks. Take the case where it is not raining and the home team wins, which is row 3. "The home team wins whenever it is raining" is true: nothing was promised about dry days. Its contrapositive, "if the home team does not win it is not raining", is also true, vacuously. But its converse, "if the home team wins it is raining", is false, since the team won in the dry; and its inverse, "if it is not raining the home team does not win", is false for the same reason. One concrete case, and it exhibits the difference the table proves in general.

A second line worth adding: the converse and the inverse have identical columns, so they are equivalent to each other. They are contrapositives of one another.

a. Five quantified translations (7.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 1.4. C(x) = x has a cat, D(x) = x has a dog, F(x) = x has a ferret, domain = the students in the class. Because the domain is already the students, no S(x) is needed and no arrow appears.

i. ∃x (C(x) ∧ D(x) ∧ F(x))
ii. ∀x (C(x) ∨ D(x) ∨ F(x))
iii. ∃x (C(x) ∧ F(x) ∧ ¬D(x))
iv. ¬∃x (C(x) ∧ D(x) ∧ F(x)), equivalently ∀x ¬(C(x) ∧ D(x) ∧ F(x))
v. ∃x C(x) ∧ ∃y D(y) ∧ ∃z F(z)

Part v is the one that separates candidates. "For each of the three animals there is a student who has it" allows a different student for each animal, so it needs three separate quantifiers. Writing ∃x (C(x) ∧ D(x) ∧ F(x)) would say one student has all three, which is part i, not part v.

Part iv is the negation of part i, which is worth saying: it makes the pair easy to check and shows the structure was seen rather than guessed.

b. i. When f ∘ g = g ∘ f (2 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 4.3. With f(x) = ax + b and g(x) = cx + d:

(f ∘ g)(x) = f(cx + d) = a(cx + d) + b = acx + ad + b
(g ∘ f)(x) = g(ax + b) = c(ax + b) + d = acx + bc + d

The x terms already agree, so the two are equal for every x exactly when the constants agree:

ad + b = bc + d

That single equation is both necessary and sufficient, which is what the question asked for.

b. ii. If f and f ∘ g are one-to-one, is g? (2 marks)

Yes, and here is the proof.

Proof. Suppose g(x1) = g(x2). Applying f to both sides, f(g(x1)) = f(g(x2)), that is (f ∘ g)(x1) = (f ∘ g)(x2). Since f ∘ g is one-to-one, x1 = x2. Therefore g is one-to-one. □

Note what was not used: the hypothesis that f is one-to-one never appears. The result holds from f ∘ g alone, and saying so shows the argument was followed rather than recited.

b. iii. f ∘ g and g ∘ f for x2 + 1 and x + 2 (2 marks)

(f ∘ g)(x) = f(x + 2) = (x + 2)2 + 1 = x2 + 4x + 5
(g ∘ f)(x) = g(x2 + 1) = (x2 + 1) + 2 = x2 + 3

They are not equal. One value settles it: at x = 1 the first gives 10 and the second gives 4. This identical question is set again on the 2023/2024 paper.

c. "Female and a parent implies someone's mother" (4 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 1.4. Over a domain of all people, with F(x) = x is female, P(x) = x is a parent, and M(x, y) = x is the mother of y:

∀x ((F(x) ∧ P(x)) → ∃y M(x, y))

Three things to point at. The domain is all people, so the universal quantifier takes an arrow. "Someone's mother" is an existence claim about a second person, so it needs its own ∃y inside. And the ∃y sits inside the implication, because a different child may serve each mother.

a. Why (A × B) × (C × D) and A × (B × C) × D differ (3.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 2.3.

The point is the shape of the elements, not their number. A typical element of the first is ((a, b), (c, d)): an ordered pair whose two entries are themselves ordered pairs. A typical element of the second is (a, (b, c), d): an ordered triple whose middle entry is a pair.

A pair of pairs is not a triple, so no element of one set is an element of the other, and the two sets are not equal. The Cartesian product is not associative.

What is true. The two sets have the same size, n(A)n(B)n(C)n(D) either way, and there is an obvious one-to-one correspondence between them. Equal size is not equality, and saying both halves is what a 3.5-mark answer looks like.

b. C++ program for the power set (6 marks)

Quoted as printed, and answered with a compiled and run listing, in section 11.3. The method in one line: count a mask from 0 to 2n − 1 and print element i whenever bit i of the mask is set. That enumeration produces the eight subsets in exactly the order the paper prints them, including the empty set as { }.

c. The first De Morgan law by set-builder notation (3 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 2.2.

Note on the printed line first. The paper prints the law with the overbar sitting over B alone and with a dash where an equals sign belongs. The law being asked for is that the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements, and that is what is established here.

To prove: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.

Proof, by a chain of equivalences on an arbitrary element.

x ∈ (A ∩ B)′
≡ ¬(x ∈ A ∩ B)     [definition of complement]
≡ ¬(x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ B)     [definition of intersection]
≡ ¬(x ∈ A) ∨ ¬(x ∈ B)     [De Morgan for propositions, section 1.3]
≡ x ∈ A′ ∨ x ∈ B′     [definition of complement, twice]
≡ x ∈ A′ ∪ B′     [definition of union]

Since an arbitrary x belongs to one side exactly when it belongs to the other, the two sets are equal. □

Name the step that does the work. The whole proof is the propositional De Morgan law with set membership substituted for the propositions, and saying so is the point of the question.

d. i. Bit string of the complement (2.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 2.3. With U = {1, ..., 10}, the set {1, 3, 5, 7, 9} is 1010101010. The complement flips every bit:

0101010101, which is {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}

The complement is a bitwise NOT, which is why bit strings are used for sets in the first place.

d. ii. Union and intersection by bit strings (2.5 marks)

{1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is 1111100000 and {1, 3, 5, 7, 9} is 1010101010.

Union is bitwise OR, 1 where either has a 1: 1111101010, which is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9}
Intersection is bitwise AND, 1 only where both have a 1: 1010100000, which is {1, 3, 5}

Check by eye: the intersection is the odd numbers up to 5, which is exactly what the two sets share.

a. Truth values over the real numbers (4 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 1.4. Each answer needs a witness if it is true and a counterexample if it is false; the verdict alone is worth little.

i. ∃x(x3 = −1). TRUE. Witness x = −1, since (−1)3 = −1.

ii. ∃x(x4 < x2). TRUE. Witness x = 1/2: x4 = 1/16 and x2 = 1/4, and 1/16 < 1/4. In general it holds for every x strictly between −1 and 1 other than 0.

iii. ∀x((−x)2 = x2). TRUE. For any real x, (−x)2 = (−1)2x2 = x2.

iv. ∀x(2x > x). FALSE. Counterexample x = 0, which gives 0 > 0, false. Also x = −1, which gives −2 > −1, false. The claim is only true for positive x, and this is the part where the domain "all real numbers" is doing the work.

b. R1 to R6 on {1, 2, 3, 4} (7.5 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 3.2. One table answers all five parts and is far easier to mark than five sentences.

RelationReflexiveSymmetricAntisymmetricTransitive
R1nononono
R2noyesnono
R3yesyesnono
R4nonoyesyes
R5yesnoyesyes
R6nonoyesyes

i and v. Reflexive: R3 and R5. Only these contain all four loops (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4).

ii. Symmetric: R2 and R3. In each, every pair appears with its reverse.

iii. Antisymmetric: R4, R5 and R6. None of them contains both (a, b) and (b, a) for two different elements.

iv. Transitive: R4, R5 and R6. Every composable pair of arrows has its shortcut present.

On the repeated part. The paper asks "Which of these relations are reflexive?" as part i and again as part v. Answer it twice, identically, and add one line: the intended part was almost certainly irreflexive or asymmetric, and if irreflexive was meant the answer is R4 and R6, the two containing no loop at all. That line costs nothing and covers both readings.

c. C++ isPerfectSquare by binary search (6 marks)

Quoted as printed, and answered with a compiled and run listing, in section 11.3. The method in one line: search the range [1, num], compare the square of the midpoint with num, keep the half that can still contain the answer, and return the midpoint on a hit or −1 when the range empties. The function keeps the paper's own name and capitalisation, and its return type is int rather than bool, because the question asks for the square root to be returned.

blocks.problem: Quoted whole, as printed, in section 6.3. The scenario: 24 vertices, 30 edges, five vertices of degree 4, seven pendant vertices, seven of degree 2, and every other vertex of degree 3 or 4.
blocks.working:
a. How many vertices of degree 4? (4 marks)

Not five. The question says five vertices are of degree 4 and then says all other vertices have degree 3 or 4, so more of them are hiding in the remainder. Work it out.

degree sum = 2|E| = 2 × 30 = 60     [Handshaking]
named vertices = 5 + 7 + 7 = 19, leaving 24 − 19 = 5
their degree = 4 × 5 + 1 × 7 + 2 × 7 = 20 + 7 + 14 = 41
degree left for the last five = 60 − 41 = 19

Let four of them have degree 4 and three of them degree 3, with four + three = 5 and 4(four) + 3(three) = 19. Substituting, 4(four) + 3(5 − four) = 19, so four = 4 and three = 1.

So the graph has 5 + 4 = 9 vertices of degree 4.

Check: the full degree list is five 4s, seven 1s, seven 2s, four 4s and one 3, summing to 20 + 7 + 14 + 16 + 3 = 60, and the vertices count 5 + 7 + 7 + 4 + 1 = 24. Both agree.

b. Degree-4 vertices in the corresponding complete graph (1 mark)

The corresponding complete graph on the same 24 vertices is K24, in which every vertex is joined to all 23 others, so every degree is 23.

Therefore the number of vertices of degree 4 in it is 0. State the reading in the same breath: "taking the corresponding complete graph to be K24". A one-mark part rewards the observation, not a calculation.

c. Does the Handshaking theorem hold here? (3 marks)

Statement. In any undirected graph, Σ deg(v) = 2|E|: the degrees sum to twice the number of edges, because each edge contributes exactly one to the degree of each of its two ends.

Applied. Here 2|E| = 60, and the degree list found in part (a) sums to 60. The two agree, so the theorem holds for this graph.

Proof of the theorem itself. Count the pairs (v, e) where vertex v is an end of edge e. Counting by vertices gives Σ deg(v); counting by edges gives 2|E|, since every edge has exactly two ends. One quantity counted two ways must give the same total. □

A consequence worth adding: the degree sum is always even, so a graph with an odd degree sum cannot exist. That is the fact part (a) relied on.

d. C++ snippet for the remaining vertices (3 marks)

Answered with a compiled and run listing in section 11.3. The snippet computes 24 − 19 = 5 vertices left, 60 − 41 = 19 degree left to share, then solves the pair of equations in one line to print four of degree 4 and one of degree 3.

e. Handshaking in data communication (2 marks)

In a communication network model the vertices are devices and the edges are links. The theorem says the total number of link ends, that is the sum over devices of how many links each has, is exactly twice the number of links.

Two uses. Capacity planning: if a network is to have 50 links, the port counts across all devices must total 100, which sizes the hardware before anything is bought. And validation: if a device inventory reports an odd total number of ports, the inventory is wrong, because no network can have an odd total. That second use is a real error check and is the better half of the answer.

f. n vertices, n edges, no degree 0 or 1 (3 marks)

To prove: if G has n vertices and n edges and no vertex has degree 0 or 1, then every vertex has degree exactly 2.

Proof. By Handshaking, Σ deg(v) = 2|E| = 2n. No vertex has degree 0 or 1, so every one of the n vertices has degree at least 2, and therefore

Σ deg(v) ≥ 2n

But the sum equals 2n. If any single vertex had degree 3 or more, the sum would exceed 2n, since the other n − 1 vertices already contribute at least 2 each. That is impossible, so no vertex exceeds degree 2. Combined with every degree being at least 2, every degree is exactly 2. □

What such a graph looks like, worth one extra line: every vertex of degree 2 and n edges means G is a disjoint union of cycles.

g. What it means for G and H to be isomorphic (1.5 marks)

G and H are isomorphic when there is a one-to-one correspondence between their vertex sets that preserves adjacency: two vertices are joined in G exactly when their partners are joined in H. In plain words, they are the same graph drawn differently, with the vertices renamed.

The consequence a marker looks for: isomorphic graphs must agree on every structural property, so the same number of vertices, the same number of edges and the same list of degrees. Any disagreement in those proves they are not isomorphic.

a. Three traversals of the given tree (6 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 7.3, where the tree is redrawn and each traversal is walked step by step. The tree has 17 vertices: a is the root with children b and c; b has d, e, f; e has j, k; k has n, o; c has g, h, i; h has l, m; m has p, q.

i. Preorder visits the root, then each subtree in turn:

a, b, d, e, j, k, n, o, f, c, g, h, l, m, p, q, i

ii. Inorder visits the leftmost subtree, then the root, then the remaining subtrees:

d, b, j, e, n, k, o, f, a, g, c, l, h, p, m, q, i

iii. Postorder visits every subtree first and the root last:

d, j, n, o, k, e, f, b, g, l, p, q, m, h, i, c, a

Two checks worth the ten seconds. All three lists have 17 entries. Preorder starts at the root and postorder ends at it.

b. i. The rooted tree of the expression (2 marks)

Quoted as printed in section 7.3. Two superscript characters in the printed expression could not be read at any available resolution, so this answers the plain reading (3 − 4 · 2) − (5 + (5 − 2)) and says in one line what changes otherwise.

The tree. The root is the outer subtraction. Its left subtree is 3 − 4 · 2, whose root is a subtraction with 3 on the left and a multiplication of 4 and 2 on the right. Its right subtree is 5 + (5 − 2), whose root is an addition with 5 on the left and a subtraction of 5 and 2 on the right.

Its value: (3 − 8) − (5 + 3) = −5 − 8 = −13.

If the two marks are exponents, the tree gains two exponent nodes, one above each bracketed group, and the values change; the structure of the answer does not.

b. iv. Prefix notation (2 marks)

− − 3 · 4 2 + 5 − 5 2

b. v. Postfix notation (2 marks)

3 4 2 · − 5 5 2 − + −

Both are read off the tree, prefix by visiting each node before its subtrees and postfix by visiting it after. Neither is the other reversed, and neither is produced by moving the symbols of the infix expression about by eye.

b. vi. Leaves of a quinary tree of height 3 (2.5 marks)

Say what is determined first. A quinary tree of height 3 could have as few as 3 leaves; what m and h fix is the maximum. With m = 5 and h = 3:

leaves = mh = 53 = 125

Cross-check by the other formula. The full quinary tree of height 3 has internal vertices 1 + 5 + 25 = 31, and l = (m − 1)i + 1 = 4 × 31 + 1 = 125. The two agree.

b. vii. Prove the mh bound (3 marks)

Proof, by induction on the height h.

Base case, h = 0. A tree of height 0 is a single vertex, which is both root and leaf: 1 leaf, and m0 = 1.

Hypothesis. Every m-ary tree of height k has at most mk leaves.

Step. Let T have height k + 1. Removing the root leaves at most m subtrees, one per child, each of height at most k, so each has at most mk leaves by the hypothesis. Every leaf of T lies in one of them, so T has at most m × mk = mk+1 leaves. □

When the bound is attained: exactly when the tree is full and every leaf sits at level h. Saying so shows the bound is sharp, not merely true.
